intro.heading: The home-tutor question for 0478, answered with numbers
paragraphs: Hiring a tutor who comes to the house is a normal arrangement in Dubai and there is nothing wrong with it. The market is well developed, the rates are published in places if you look, and for younger children the case is strong. For Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science specifically, two things make the in-home version harder than it looks, and both are worth knowing before you start calling numbers in a community group.

The first is price, and the reason behind it. Published figures for Dubai put in-home one-to-one tuition at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour: Bestimate's 2026 rate table for the city gives AED 180 to 350, and independent home tutors advertise AED 200 to 500. Qualified online one-to-one sits lower, around AED 150 to 300, with Unitors listing IGCSE tuition from AED 150. That gap is not a difference in teaching quality. It is a tutor's drive time being paid for, which in this city is a real cost for them and a large one for you.

The second is supply. A tutor who can teach both 0478 papers properly is a narrower population than a tutor who can help with Python. The qualification examines computer systems in one paper and algorithms, programming, databases and Boolean logic in the other, with no coursework component at all, and the second paper is where most families' problems sit. Inside a twenty-minute radius of any one Dubai community, the number of people who have taught that second paper to examination standard and are free at six in the evening is small. Several of the families who contact us have already discovered this.

IB Gram's answer is to drop the radius rather than the standard. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on a fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time, matched to the programming language your child's school teaches. We do not send a tutor to a Dubai address at all; visiting a family's home is a service we run only in India, and saying so plainly is better than letting a parent book a trial expecting a doorbell.

For a subject built on code, the shared screen is also the better tool. A tutor can see the student's actual editor, run the program, break it on purpose to show what the error reveals, then convert it into the handwritten pseudocode the exam demands, with every annotated file saved and sent afterwards. By February the student holds a folder of their own worked examples. A visiting tutor leans over the same laptop for an hour and leaves nothing behind.

What follows is the detail a family needs to make this decision on numbers rather than on impressions: the hour itemised into its parts, how fast a local shortlist shrinks once you filter for both papers, what the drive actually costs in a Dubai late afternoon, how group classes and tuition centres compare, the evidence you should expect to see at six weeks, where Computer Science sits in Ministry of Education equivalency, and the seven questions worth putting to any tutor before money changes hands.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-computer-science-0.programmesIntro: Three programme stages matter for this decision, because the right spend on a Year 10 student and a Year 11 student eight weeks from a paper are different products. Each note is about Dubai specifically.

programmes.name: Cambridge Upper Secondary: Computer Science 0478
programmes.description: Two written papers of equal weight, one on computer systems and one on algorithms, programming, databases and Boolean logic. No coursework, and nothing assessed at a keyboard. Tutoring value concentrates in exam technique, because most students already have more content than their marks suggest.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's private sector enrolled 387,441 students across 227 schools in 2024-25, with seven more schools opening for 2026-27 adding 16,846 places. For computing families the relevant detail is narrower: not every school enters candidates for 0478, some offer ICT 0417 instead, and a few put both in the same option column. Confirm which your child's school actually enters before buying tuition for either.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme: Design and digital units
programmes.description: The IB alternative in the same age band, where computing is taught through design cycles and internally assessed against criteria rather than through external written papers. Students develop genuine project skill and rarely meet pseudocode conventions or handwritten algorithm work.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai has a large IB sector, with International Baccalaureate schools taking 7 per cent of private enrolment in 2024-25 and three new IB schools among those opening for 2026-27. Families moving a child from MYP into Year 10 or 11 of a British-curriculum school should expect the examination discipline to be the gap, not the subject knowledge, and should budget a short diagnostic block rather than a full term.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level Computer Science 9618
programmes.description: The continuation, with deeper data structures, logic and system software, plus a programming project at full A Level. It assumes fluency in one text-based language from the start of Year 12 rather than building it.
programmes.countryNote: Because Dubai students choose between A Level and the IB Diploma in the spring of Year 11, the money question arrives early: is tuition in Year 11 buying a grade or buying readiness for Year 12. Where a student intends to continue with computing, the summer between the two years is usually a better spend than extra sessions in May, and we will say so rather than selling the extra sessions.

sections.heading: What you are actually paying for in an in-home hour
paragraphs: The hourly rate for a visiting tutor is not one thing. It bundles the teaching hour, the drive in both directions, the fuel and tolls, the risk that a cancelled lesson leaves a hole in the tutor's evening that cannot be filled, and the preparation for a named syllabus. Online delivery removes several of those components outright. That is the whole of the price difference, and it is worth seeing itemised rather than argued about.

The published Dubai figures make the pattern visible. Bestimate's 2026 rate table for the city puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 an hour, independent home tutors advertise AED 200 to 500, and qualified online one-to-one runs around AED 150 to 300, with Unitors listing IGCSE tuition from AED 150. Monthly packages advertised locally include AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions and AED 799 for eight online sessions. Those figures come from the providers themselves as of October 2026; none of them is ours.

There is a hidden component that never appears on a rate card and matters more in computing than anywhere else: the cost of a mismatch. A tutor who has not taught the second paper of this syllabus will spend paid hours reading the specification. At AED 250 an hour, three sessions of that is AED 750 spent on somebody's preparation rather than your child's marks. The useful comparison is not rate against rate; it is total spend against measurable movement.

The table itemises the hour so a family can see which parts they are funding in each format. It is deliberately unflattering about the parts of online delivery that are genuinely worse, because a comparison that only runs one way is not a comparison.

sections.heading: The twenty-minute radius problem
paragraphs: Hiring locally means hiring from everyone willing to drive to your community at the time you need. In practice that is a short list, and the list gets shorter with every constraint you add. For 0478 the constraints are unusually specific: the tutor needs to teach both papers, needs to work in the programming language the school uses, and needs to be free in the narrow band between the school bus arriving and homework starting.

Think about what each filter removes. Tutors who advertise computing but really teach ICT: removed. Tutors fluent in one language but not the school's: removed. Tutors who can teach algorithms but have never covered database design or Boolean logic, the two topics schools reach late: removed. Tutors free at 6pm on the one weekday your child has nothing else: removed. What is left in a single Dubai community is frequently nobody, and the family then compromises on the filter that matters most rather than on the convenience.

Across a national pool working over video the same filters leave a real choice, and the compromise moves to something smaller, usually the exact time of the slot. That is the trade IB Gram asks families to make. It is also why we tell you before a trial if the only available specialist does not know the school's language, rather than discovering it in week three.

One honest caveat. A wider pool is not automatically a better tutor, and an online platform that matches by availability alone is no better than a neighbour with a leaflet. The question to put to any provider, including us, is which of your child's two papers the proposed tutor has taught, and to which year groups.

sections.heading: Travel time in Dubai, counted properly
paragraphs: A 5pm lesson in a villa community is rarely a 5pm commitment for the tutor. Leaving enough margin to arrive reliably across Al Khail Road or Sheikh Zayed Road in the late afternoon means setting off around 4pm, and the return leg lands them home after seven. Two hours and a half of a working day for one paid hour. Multiply that across a week and the arithmetic behind the published in-home premium stops looking like a markup.

The family carries its own version of the same problem. Students bussing from communities on the southern corridor or the eastern edge to schools elsewhere in the city often arrive home well after four, which pushes a realistic start past five. Co-curricular commitments fill the next hour. The genuinely available windows in a Dubai school week are narrower than the calendar suggests, and a visiting tutor has to fit inside the same gaps while also driving to them.

Then there is the failure mode. A visiting tutor delayed by an accident on the Al Khail arrives at 5:40pm for a 5pm lesson, and the hour becomes thirty-five rushed minutes. Over a term, two or three of those are normal. An online slot is exposed to a connection problem instead, which is less frequent and recoverable within a minute or two.

None of this argues that in-home tuition fails. It argues that the travel is a real part of what is bought, and that for a subject where the materials live on a screen anyway, paying for the drive buys very little. We are explicit about our position: IB Gram does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE, because the version we can run well is the online one.

sections.heading: Why code is the strongest case for a shared screen
paragraphs: Most subjects lose something when they move to video. Computing gains. The work already lives inside a screen, and the two activities a 0478 student most needs, running code and converting it into handwritten exam form, are both easier when the tutor can see and control the same editor rather than peering at a laptop from the side of a dining table.

A live session will typically run a student's own program, break it deliberately by changing a condition, and ask what the error message reveals about the logic. Then the same algorithm gets written out by hand in pseudocode and traced in a table, because that is the form the exam requires and nothing in a student's normal coding life ever asks for it. Both halves of that happen in front of the student rather than being described to them.

The artefact matters as much as the lesson. Annotated pseudocode, the trace table as it was built, and the corrected program are saved and sent afterwards, which means by February the student is revising from their own worked examples rather than from a textbook. Parents can see the file too, which is a more honest progress report than a verbal summary at the door.

The table sets the two formats against each other task by task. Three rows favour the room, and they are included because this decision deserves a straight answer rather than a sales pitch. A parent choosing in-home tuition for a thirteen-year-old who will not settle to a screen is making a reasonable choice, and no comparison table should pretend otherwise.

sections.heading: Group classes and tuition centres: the third option
paragraphs: Dubai families weighing a home tutor usually also look at a tuition centre or a small group class, because the per-student rate is lower. For some subjects that is sound value. For 0478 it is the weakest of the three options, and the reason is structural rather than a matter of teaching quality.

A group works when the students share a gap. In computer science they rarely do. One student cannot trace a loop, another cannot convert hexadecimal, a third programs fluently and writes unmarkable prose on the systems paper. An hour spent on any one of those is an hour two of them did not need. The group then defaults to covering content everyone has already met, which feels productive and moves nobody.

Centres with premises in Dubai also sit under a different regulatory regime from individual tutors. A tuition business with staff and premises requires an educational services permit for a training institute from KHDA, with initial approval first and annual renewal, while an individual tutor needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit. The two are not interchangeable, and a centre's permit says nothing about whether the person teaching your child holds one.

Where a group does earn its place is early coverage in Year 10, before gaps diverge, and occasionally for a shared theory revision block on the systems paper, where every candidate needs the same six topics. For algorithm and logic work in the spring of Year 11, one-to-one is the format that matches the problem, because by then no two students in a room are losing marks in the same place.

sections.heading: What a parent should see after six weeks
paragraphs: Tutoring is bought on faith and should be judged on evidence. For 0478 the evidence is unusually concrete, because the things that cost marks are countable. A parent paying from AED 150 an hour upward is entitled to see movement in specific places rather than to be told the sessions are going well.

The first is trace table completeness. In week one most students produce tables with skipped iterations and missing intermediate values. By week five, three timed tables out of three should be complete, even if a value or two is wrong. That single change is usually worth more Paper 2 marks than any amount of new content.

The second is the scored topic list from the diagnostic. Weak rows should have moved and the list should be shorter, with the remaining rows named. The third is answer grain on the systems paper: a two-mark describe question answered with two distinct technical points rather than a paragraph. The fourth, for students who were avoiding code, is simply whether they now write an algorithm by hand without being asked twice.

At six weeks we compare the first marked work with the most recent and give a view in writing, including when the view is that the plan should change or that a different tutor would be a better fit. Changing tutor at a review point costs nothing. Continuing for a term because nobody looked at the evidence is the expensive outcome.

sections.heading: Does Computer Science count towards Ministry of Education equivalency?
paragraphs: Families planning a UAE university route ask this, and the answer is specific enough to be worth stating carefully. For the British track, the published requirement is five accredited subjects at GCSE or IGCSE with a grade no lower than E or grade 3, plus either one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

Computer Science 0478 is an accredited IGCSE subject, so it can sit inside that count of five. One competitor page ranking for these queries states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects, which does not match the published rule; the number in the Ministry's clarification is five. That is the kind of detail worth checking against the source rather than taking from a tutoring website, including this one.

For the American track the same clarification sets out different requirements: English proficiency evidenced by a score of 5 in IELTS academic, 61 in TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and at least 450 in SAT Mathematics. For the International Baccalaureate, no points threshold has been verified from the Ministry's own pages, so no figure appears here; ask the Ministry or the emirate's attestation authority directly.

Two boundaries matter. Equivalency is assessed by the Ministry of Education, not by any tutoring provider, and nobody should present it as something they perform or can expedite. And tutoring is not a requirement for equivalency, university admission or school progression. Anyone implying otherwise is manufacturing urgency around a regulatory process.

sections.heading: Seven questions to ask before you hire anyone for 0478
paragraphs: Most of the risk in this purchase is removed in one conversation. The questions below are the ones that separate a computing specialist from a general tutor who lists computing, and they work equally well on us as on anyone advertising in a community group.

Start with the papers. Which of the two have you taught, and to which year groups? A tutor who talks only about programming is describing half the qualification. Then the language: which text-based language do you teach, and will you work in the one the school uses? Then the late topics: how do you teach database design and Boolean logic? If the answer is vague, those marks will stay lost.

Then the mechanics. How is work set between sessions, and is handwritten algorithm practice part of it? How will I see progress, and when? What happens if the match does not work? And finally the permit question, which is entirely reasonable to ask in this market: do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023? It is issued free of charge for two years, so there is no cost reason for a tutor not to hold one.

Our own answers are on this page. IB Gram delivers one-to-one online lessons in the UAE and no home visits; holds no accreditation from KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education or Cambridge; occupies no UAE office; publishes no price list, because a free first lesson and a written plan produce a more honest quote; and promises no grades, because examiners mark a script written on one morning.

faqs.question: Can IB Gram provide a tutor who comes to our house in Dubai for 0478?
faqs.answer: No. Sending a tutor to a family's address is something we do only in India, and every UAE lesson is delivered one-to-one over live video on a fixed Gulf Standard Time slot. We state it plainly because the search term is a home tutor and a parent should not book a trial expecting a doorbell. For this subject the online format is also the stronger one: the tutor sees and controls the same editor, runs the student's code, and sends the annotated pseudocode and trace tables afterwards.

faqs.question: How much does in-home computer science tuition cost per month in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Advertised in-home packages in the city include AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour sessions, while online packages advertise around AED 799 a month for eight sessions. On an hourly basis, Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table gives AED 180 to 350 for in-home one-to-one and independent tutors advertise up to AED 500, against AED 150 to 300 for qualified online one-to-one. Those are the providers' own published figures as of October 2026. IB Gram quotes in AED after a free first lesson.

faqs.question: How many tutors near us have actually taught both 0478 papers?
faqs.answer: Fewer than families expect. Filter a local list by tutors who teach the systems paper as well as algorithms, who work in the language the school uses, who have covered database design and Boolean logic, and who are free in the narrow window after the school bus arrives, and a single community often has nobody left. That is the arithmetic behind online matching. Ask any provider, including us, which of the two papers the proposed tutor has taught and to which year groups.

faqs.question: Does a tutor's travel time really change what I pay?
faqs.answer: It is most of the difference between the published bands. A visiting tutor leaving at four to reach a villa community reliably for a five o'clock lesson commits well over two hours of their day for one paid hour, plus fuel and tolls, and a late cancellation usually leaves a hole they cannot fill. Published Dubai in-home rates of AED 180 to 500 an hour reflect that, against AED 150 to 300 online. The teaching in both bands can be equally good.

faqs.question: Is screen sharing really better than sitting beside my child for coding work?
faqs.answer: For algorithm and programming work, yes, and for two concrete reasons. Both people see and control the same editor, so a tutor can run the program, change a condition to break it deliberately, and show what the error reveals. And everything produced is saved: annotated pseudocode, the trace table as it was built, the corrected code. A tutor in the room leans over one laptop and leaves pencil marks. Where the room genuinely wins is with younger or very distractible students.

faqs.question: Can two children in the same house share one session?
faqs.answer: We schedule siblings back to back rather than together. A shared hour sounds efficient and works badly in this subject, because two students almost never have the same gap: one cannot trace a loop, the other cannot convert hexadecimal. Consecutive one-to-one slots give each child undivided time and still disrupt only one evening. Different subjects and different year groups are fine, and each child is reviewed on their own evidence at the six-week point.

faqs.question: What should I ask a computer science tutor before hiring them?
faqs.answer: Seven things: which of the two papers they have taught and to which year groups; which text-based language they will work in; how they teach database design and Boolean logic; whether handwritten algorithm practice is set between sessions; how and when you will see progress; whether they hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is issued free of charge for two years; and what happens if the match is wrong. Vague answers on the late topics usually mean those marks stay lost.

faqs.question: Is a tuition centre group class worth it for computer science?
faqs.answer: It is the weakest of the three formats for this subject, though it has a place. Groups work when students share a gap, and in computing they rarely do, so an hour spent on one student's problem is an hour the others did not need. Centres also sit under a different regime: a tuition business with premises in Dubai requires an educational services permit for a training institute from KHDA, while an individual tutor needs the MoHRE permit. A centre's permit tells you nothing about the person teaching.

faqs.question: What progress should I see after six weeks of 0478 support?
faqs.answer: Four countable things. Trace tables completed in full rather than with skipped iterations. A shorter weak-topic list than the one from the first diagnostic. Two-mark describe questions answered with two distinct technical points instead of a paragraph. And handwritten algorithm work produced without being asked twice. Those are visible in the scripts, and we put a written view at six weeks including when the honest view is to change tutor or stop. No tutor can promise a grade.

faqs.question: Does IGCSE Computer Science count towards UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: It is an accredited IGCSE subject, so it can form part of the published British-track requirement: five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no lower than grade E or grade 3, plus one A Level at grade E or two AS Levels. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. One ranking competitor states that six subjects are required, which does not match the published rule. Equivalency is assessed by the Ministry of Education, not by any tutoring provider, so verify your child's combination through the Ministry's own channel.

faqs.question: Can we buy a short block of sessions rather than committing to a term?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for many Year 10 families it is the right purchase. A diagnostic block of three or four sessions scores the student across the syllabus topics, tests one handwritten algorithm and one trace table, and ends with a written view rather than an automatic renewal. Sometimes that view is that no further tuition is needed yet, which is a legitimate outcome. Nothing rolls over without a decision, and there is no term paid in advance.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor and my child are not a good fit?
faqs.answer: You say so and we change the tutor, at no cost, at the six-week review or earlier if it is clearly wrong. A mismatch in this subject is usually specific rather than personal: the tutor is strong on theory and light on algorithms, or works in a different language from the school. Naming which it is makes the second match better. What we try to avoid is a family continuing for a term because nobody looked at the evidence and the sessions felt pleasant enough.

faqs.question: What equipment does my child need at home for online computing lessons?
faqs.answer: A laptop with a working camera and microphone, a stable connection, headphones, and whatever development environment the school uses already installed. A tablet is workable for theory sessions and poor for code. Paper and a pen matter as much as the laptop, because algorithm work is set by hand. No software purchase is required from us, and we send a link rather than asking anyone to install a platform.

faqs.question: Can sessions be scheduled around Dubai school bus timings?
faqs.answer: That is usually the first scheduling constraint we work around. Students bussing from southern or eastern communities to schools elsewhere in the city often arrive home well after four, which pushes a realistic start past five, and co-curricular commitments then fill the next hour. The busiest slots we hold for Year 11 sit between seven and half past eight. The slot is fixed weekly, moves for Ramadan if a family asks, and continues across time zones when a family travels.

faqs.question: Why does IB Gram not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE?
faqs.answer: Because the version we can run well at scale is the online one, and pretending otherwise would mean sending whoever is nearest rather than whoever teaches the syllabus. Visiting tutors are a service we run only in India, where the operating model supports it. In the UAE every lesson is one-to-one over live video, which removes the travel component from the published AED 180 to 500 in-home band and replaces a twenty-minute radius with a national pool of specialists.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-computer-science-0.tutorsIntro: These tutors teach Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science online across Dubai and the Gulf. Each works to a two-year map rather than week to week, which is what makes the difference between covering the syllabus and being ready to sit it.

intro.heading: Two years, six terms and the marks that go missing in between
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science is a two-year course assessed by two written papers of equal weight, and the mistake families make is treating it as a subject you revise at the end. The systems paper rewards precision that takes months to build. The algorithms paper rewards handwritten fluency with pseudocode and trace tables, which is a habit rather than a body of knowledge, and habits do not form in April. A student who starts practising algorithm writing in the spring of Year 11 is learning a motor skill under exam pressure.

So the useful question for an online tutor is not what to teach this week but where the student is against a two-year map. Which of the six systems topics have been covered and scored. Whether database design and Boolean logic have been met at all, since schools frequently reach them late. Whether the student has ever written an algorithm by hand without a keyboard in front of them. Those three answers shape a plan; a request to help with computer science does not.

That is why the first session is a diagnostic rather than a lesson. The student scores themselves across the ten syllabus topics, writes one short algorithm by hand, and completes one trace table from given code. Twenty minutes produces a ranked list of what is actually costing marks, which is usually different from the parent's theory and almost always different from the student's. Everything after that is built on that list and reviewed against it.

Delivery is online, one-to-one, over live video on a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses; home visits are a service we run only in India. For a subject where the work already lives inside a screen, that is the stronger format rather than a compromise: the tutor sees and controls the same editor, runs the student's own program, breaks it deliberately, and converts it into exam form alongside, with every file saved and sent afterwards.

There is a second reason the two-year view matters in this emirate specifically. Dubai schools differ widely in when they teach the algorithms content: some spread programming constructs across Year 10, others leave most of the second paper to Year 11, and a few reach database design and Boolean logic only in the final term. A plan written from the syllabus assumes an order the school may not be following. A plan written from the department's own scheme of work, checked against what the student can actually do unaided, is the one that survives contact with February.

This page sets out the two-year map, what the diagnostic contains, what gets set between lessons, where we stand on AI tools in a programming subject, how the mandatory UAE subjects affect a computing option block, how retakes and private-candidate entries work, how Dubai families use Ramadan and the long holidays, and the cases where online tuition is the wrong answer and we will say so rather than take the booking.

sections.heading: The two-year map, term by term
paragraphs: Most tutoring plans for this subject are written week to week, which is why they run out of road in March. A better plan starts from the end: two written papers, ten topics, and a set of handwritten skills that need months of light repetition rather than a block of intensive work. From there the six terms allocate themselves fairly naturally, and a family can see at any point whether they are ahead or behind.

The shape is simple. Year 10 is for coverage and for building handwritten habits while nothing is at stake. Term one of Year 11 is for finishing the systems topics and scoring each one honestly. Term two is for the topics schools reach late, databases and Boolean logic, and for full papers under timing. Term three is for question analysis and for the second half of each paper, where fatigue costs marks that knowledge has already earned.

What this map mainly does is expose gaps early enough to be cheap. A student who has never written an algorithm by hand is a six-week problem in October and a serious problem in April. A student who has not met database design is a two-session problem in January and an unanswered question in the exam. The table below is the version we give parents, because it lets them ask the school a specific question rather than a general one.

Schools differ, sometimes substantially, in when they teach the algorithms content. Ask the head of computing for the department's two-year scheme of work rather than for the syllabus. The syllabus tells you what will be examined; only the scheme of work tells you when your child will have been taught it.

sections.heading: What the first diagnostic session actually contains
paragraphs: A diagnostic is only useful if it produces decisions. Ours takes about twenty minutes and has three parts, each chosen because it reveals something a report card does not. The student scores themselves on each of the ten syllabus topics, writes one short algorithm by hand from a worded specification, and completes one trace table from code they have not seen.

The self-scoring is more reliable than parents expect, provided the question is specific. Asked whether they understand data transmission, a student says yes. Asked whether they can explain the difference between a parity check, a checksum and a check digit without looking, the same student usually says no, and that is the row that gets a session. Vague confidence collapses under a concrete question, which is the entire design of the sheet.

The handwritten algorithm is diagnostic in a different way. It shows whether the student declares variables, closes loops explicitly, and writes conditions in full, or whether they produce something a machine would tolerate and a mark scheme cannot read. The trace table shows whether they record intermediate values or only the final answer. Those two artefacts, between them, predict Paper 2 performance better than any mock grade.

The output is a ranked list with the two or three highest-return items at the top, and it is sent to the parent as well as used by the tutor. Six weeks later the same sheet is scored again, which is how the review stays honest rather than impressionistic.

sections.heading: What happens between the lessons
paragraphs: A weekly hour is a small part of a week. The work set between sessions is what makes it count, and in this subject that work has a particular character: short, frequent, handwritten and marked. An hour of set work spread across three evenings beats a single long session, because the skills being built are recall and form rather than comprehension.

The rotation is deliberately narrow. One week is a handwritten algorithm task from a worded specification, roughly twenty-five minutes. The next is a timed set of theory questions on a named topic, marked against the mark allocation rather than for general accuracy. Running through both, every week without exception, are three trace tables, because completeness only becomes automatic through repetition and students will not do them voluntarily.

Marking happens in the gap between lessons rather than during them, which is the single biggest difference between an hour that teaches and an hour that checks homework. The student arrives at the session with the script already annotated, and the live time is spent on the two faults that cost most, with one paragraph or one algorithm rebuilt in front of them.

Parents get a short note every second session saying what was set, what came back and what moved. The table sets out the standard rotation so a family can see what a month of work looks like before they buy it. Where a student is not doing the set work, we raise it at the second session rather than at the six-week review, because a weekly hour with no work between it is an expensive way to check homework.

sections.heading: AI tools, honest practice and what a tutor will not do
paragraphs: This has become the most important conversation in computing tuition, and it deserves a direct position rather than a policy paragraph. A student can now obtain working code for almost any school task in seconds. That capability is useful in life and actively harmful during this particular course, for a reason that has nothing to do with morality: the examination is handwritten and closed, and a student who has never produced an algorithm unaided has not practised the thing being tested.

Our position is straightforward. A tutor never hands a student finished code to submit, and never uses a generator to do the student's set work. Where a student has clearly submitted something they did not produce, the tutor says so and the session is spent writing the same solution from scratch, by hand, until the student can do it without help. Schools have their own rules on acceptable use for homework, and parents should ask for the school's policy in writing rather than assume.

There is a legitimate use that we do teach. Reading unfamiliar code critically, spotting where a generated solution does something subtly wrong, and explaining why it fails a specification is a genuine skill and good preparation for the kind of question that asks a candidate to find the error in somebody else's algorithm. Used that way the tool is a source of flawed code to diagnose, which is exactly what Paper 2 provides.

The broader boundary applies across everything we do. Work submitted to a school or a board must be the candidate's own. A tutor teaches, demonstrates on unrelated problems, reviews and explains. Nobody here produces material for submission, and no tutor can promise a grade, because examiners mark a script written on one morning.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside a computing option
paragraphs: This is the part of a Dubai timetable that families from the UK or South Asia consistently underestimate, and it has a direct effect on whether a student can take both computing subjects. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The requirements are specific rather than nominal. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education must hold the relevant KHDA approval to teach those subjects.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. The practical consequence for a computing family is simple arithmetic: those blocks are fixed, so the option columns around them are tighter than in a UK school, and computer science and ICT often compete for the same slot.

One further constraint is worth knowing before buying tuition in these subjects: for the mandatory UAE subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited. That is a real limit on how any provider may describe Arabic, Islamic Education or Social Studies tutoring, and it is why we describe support in those subjects as practice aligned to the school's own material rather than as a parallel programme.

sections.heading: Retakes, the November series and the private-candidate route
paragraphs: Not every 0478 story ends well in June, and the options afterwards are more open than families assume. Cambridge runs IGCSE examinations in both a June and a November series, so a single subject can be retaken within six months rather than a year. The decision is worth making quickly, because entries close months before the papers and the school's internal deadline sits earlier again.

A retake plan should start from the previous attempt rather than from the syllabus. Where a school can provide a breakdown of performance by question or by component, that breakdown is the plan: a student who lost most marks on the algorithms paper does not need to re-cover the systems topics, and six weeks spent on trace tables, database design and logic is usually a better investment than a second full year of lessons.

Students who have left school, or whose school does not enter candidates for the series they need, can sit as private candidates through an examination centre that accepts external entries. This is an administrative question with real deadlines, and it is the school or the centre that answers it, not a tutoring provider. Ask the centre about entry windows, fees and which series they run before building any study plan around a date.

For students taking Pearson Edexcel subjects alongside Cambridge ones, the calendars differ. Pearson runs May or June and November series, with the November 2026 timetable running to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results issued to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students the following day, and November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables that may be revised, so plan against the live official timetable rather than a restated date.

sections.heading: Time zones, Ramadan and the long holidays
paragraphs: A two-year plan has to survive a calendar that includes a long summer, Eid, Ramadan and frequent family travel. Online delivery is what makes that possible, and the families who get most from it are the ones who use the breaks deliberately rather than pausing through them.

Ramadan is the clearest example. Many of our Dubai families move the session to after Iftar for the month and keep the rhythm rather than stopping for four or five weeks; others reduce to a fortnightly session and add a block in the spring break. Either works. What breaks a plan is cancelling week by week, because the set work stops and the handwritten habits decay faster than content knowledge does.

The summer is the most under-used asset in the two years. It is the only period with no school deadlines, which makes it the right time for the work that needs time and no pressure: genuine programming fluency, the topics the term never reached, and for students heading to Year 12, the forty-line program that A Level will assume. Lessons run across time zones with the slot adjusted, so a family spending six weeks abroad keeps continuity.

The table maps the year as it is actually used, which is not how a syllabus is laid out. It is also how we advise families to budget: most of the value sits in term-time consistency plus two well-used breaks, rather than in a large block of sessions in the final weeks.

sections.heading: When online tuition is the wrong answer
paragraphs: A page arguing for online delivery should be able to say where it fails, and there are three cases where we tell families not to buy it. The first is a student who will not engage with a screen. Some thirteen and fourteen-year-olds need a person in the room to stay on task, and no amount of good teaching over video compensates. For those students an in-home tutor is the better product, and since we do not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE, that means recommending something we do not sell.

The second is a student whose real problem is not the subject. Where attendance, sleep, anxiety or a diagnosed learning need is driving the marks, tutoring in computer science is a treatment for the symptom. Schools in Dubai have inclusion teams and KHDA-regulated support structures, and the conversation to have first is with the school rather than with a tutor. We say so when the diagnostic makes it obvious, and families are generally relieved rather than offended.

The third is a student who is simply behind on nothing. It happens: a parent books tuition after one disappointing mock, the diagnostic comes back strong across the ten topics, and the honest answer is that the student needs three timed papers and a conversation about pacing, not twenty paid hours. That outcome costs us a sale and keeps the one piece of information a parent most needs, which is whether the problem is real.

Where online one-to-one is the right answer, it is because the subject lives on a screen, the specialist pool is national rather than local, and the materials a student needs in February are produced and saved in November. Those are concrete advantages. They are not universal, and a provider who claims they are is selling rather than advising.

process.description: Ask the school's head of computing for the department's two-year scheme of work and send it with the last mock marks for each paper. That tells us what has actually been taught, which is frequently different from what the syllabus implies at this point in the year.

process.description: The student self-scores against the ten topics using specific questions rather than topic headings, writes one handwritten algorithm and completes one trace table. The output is a ranked list of what to fix, sent to you as well as to the tutor.

process.title: Free first lesson over live video
process.description: Sixty minutes with the matched specialist on the top item from that list. No card details are taken and nothing rolls over afterwards. Parents are welcome to listen to the opening twenty minutes.

process.description: You get a written plan showing where the student sits against the term-by-term map, which paper comes first, what is set between sessions, and what will be measurable at six weeks. Where the honest answer is a short block or none, that is what it says.

process.description: The same diagnostic sheet is scored again and compared with the original, alongside trace table completeness and timed paper performance. Continuing, switching paper, changing tutor or stopping are all normal outcomes of that review.

whyPoints.title: A diagnostic before a plan
whyPoints.description: Every engagement starts with ten topics scored against specific questions, one handwritten algorithm and one trace table. It takes twenty minutes and replaces a generic revision plan with a ranked list the family keeps.

whyPoints.description: Short handwritten tasks three evenings a week, marked in the gap so live time is spent fixing faults rather than discovering them. Three trace tables every week without exception, because completeness only becomes automatic through repetition.

whyPoints.description: No tutor hands a student finished code to submit, and no generator does the set work. Where generated code appears, the session is spent rewriting the solution by hand. Used properly, flawed code is diagnostic material rather than a shortcut.

faqs.question: How is a live online 0478 lesson different from a recorded course?
faqs.answer: A recorded course delivers content; a live lesson diagnoses and corrects. In a one-to-one session the tutor watches the student write an algorithm by hand, sees the exact point where the logic slips, and makes them rebuild it rather than explaining it again. The student's own editor is shared, so their program is run and deliberately broken to show what the error reveals. Recorded material is a useful supplement for systems topics, and it cannot tell a student why their trace table is incomplete.

faqs.question: What does the first diagnostic session cover?
faqs.answer: Three things in about twenty minutes. The student scores themselves across the ten syllabus topics using specific questions rather than headings, because vague confidence collapses when asked to distinguish a parity check from a checksum. They write one short algorithm by hand from a worded specification, which reveals whether variables are declared and loops closed properly. And they complete one trace table from unseen code, which shows whether intermediate values are recorded. The output is a ranked list sent to the parent as well as the tutor.

faqs.question: What work is set between online sessions?
faqs.answer: Short, frequent and handwritten. The rotation alternates a handwritten algorithm task from a worded specification with a timed set of theory questions on the weakest systems topic, plus base conversion drills and one small database design. Running through every week are three trace tables from unseen code, because completeness only becomes automatic through repetition. Total time is about thirty-five minutes a week spread over three evenings, and everything is marked in the gap before the next session.

faqs.question: Can my child use AI tools while practising programming for 0478?
faqs.answer: Not for work that is assessed or set by the school, and not for the tutor's set work. The examination is handwritten and closed, so a student who has never produced an algorithm unaided has not practised the thing being tested. There is one legitimate use we teach: reading generated code critically and explaining exactly where it fails a specification, which is good preparation for questions that ask a candidate to find the error in somebody else's algorithm. Ask your school for its own written policy.

faqs.question: What do you do if a student hands in code they did not write?
faqs.answer: The tutor names it, without drama, and the session is spent writing the same solution from scratch by hand until the student can produce it unaided. No tutor here supplies finished code for submission. Work handed to a school or a board must be the candidate's own, and the risk of anything else falls on the student rather than on the provider. It is also self-defeating in this subject, since the paper gives no credit for code the candidate cannot reproduce.

faqs.question: Do you teach Arabic, Islamic Education or Social Studies as well?
faqs.answer: Where a tutor is available, support in those subjects is offered as practice aligned to the school's own material rather than as a parallel course. That limit is deliberate: for the mandatory UAE subjects, using different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, and KHDA requires teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education in schools to hold the relevant approval to teach them. We describe what we do accordingly and point families to the school for the curriculum itself.

faqs.question: How do the mandatory UAE subjects affect my child's option choices?
faqs.answer: They occupy fixed timetable space, which tightens the option columns around them. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab groups and weekly instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. The practical result is that computer science and ICT frequently compete for the same column rather than sitting side by side, so the Year 9 choice between them is a real decision.

faqs.question: Can my child retake 0478 in the November series?
faqs.answer: Cambridge runs IGCSE examinations in both June and November, so a single subject can be retaken within six months. Entries close months ahead of the papers and the school's internal deadline sits earlier again, so the decision has to be made quickly after results. A retake plan should start from the previous attempt rather than the syllabus: with a question-level breakdown from the school, a student who lost marks on the algorithms paper can spend six focused weeks instead of repeating a year.

faqs.question: Can a student sit 0478 as a private candidate in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Private candidate entries are made through an examination centre that accepts external candidates, and the centre sets the entry window and the fees. This is an administrative question with hard deadlines, and the centre or the school answers it rather than any tutoring provider. Confirm which series the centre runs, when entries close and what the total cost is before building a study plan around a date. We will plan the teaching around whatever the centre confirms.

faqs.question: What information do you collect about my child?
faqs.answer: The minimum needed to teach: name, year group, school, the subject and level, the marks a parent chooses to share, and contact details for the adult making the booking. Lesson materials and marked work are kept so the student and parent can access them. We ask for a parent or guardian to make the booking for a minor, we do not ask for photographs or school reports we have no use for, and anything held can be deleted on request through the contact route on the site.

faqs.question: Do lessons continue through the long summer break?
faqs.answer: They can, and the summer is the most under-used part of the two years. It is the only stretch with no school deadlines, which makes it the right time for genuine programming fluency, for topics the term never reached, and for students heading to Year 12, the forty-line program that A Level assumes from the first week. Lessons run across time zones with the slot shifted, so families spending weeks abroad keep continuity rather than restarting in September.

faqs.question: Is online tuition suitable for a student who struggles to concentrate?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and sometimes not, and we would rather say so before taking the booking. A student who needs a person in the room to stay on task often does better with a tutor present, which is a product we do not offer anywhere in the UAE. Where attention difficulties are diagnosed or suspected, the first conversation should be with the school's inclusion team rather than with a subject tutor, because tuition in computer science treats the symptom rather than the cause.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week are too many for this subject?
faqs.answer: Two is the practical ceiling for most Year 11 students, and one plus properly completed set work beats two with none. The skills that move Paper 2 marks are built by short, frequent, handwritten repetition rather than by contact hours, so a third weekly session usually displaces the homework that was doing the work. The exception is a short intensive block before a series or a resit, where two or three a week for a few weeks is reasonable and time-limited.

faqs.question: Will the tutor communicate with my child's school?
faqs.answer: Only with your involvement, and usually it is not necessary. What is genuinely useful is information flowing the other way: the department's two-year scheme of work, the question-level breakdown of a mock, and which programming language is taught. A parent can request all three in one email. Where a school is willing to share a mock breakdown directly, it makes a retake or recovery plan considerably sharper, and we will tell you exactly what to ask for.

faqs.question: What happens in a session if my child has no current homework or topic?
faqs.answer: The diagnostic list decides. That is the whole point of scoring the ten topics at the start: there is always a ranked next item, so no session is spent asking a fifteen-year-old what they would like to work on. In practice the fallback is almost always the same three things, because they pay best: trace tables from unseen code, one handwritten algorithm from a specification, and the weakest systems topic answered against the mark allocation.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-computer-science-0.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science to Year 10 and Year 11 students. Most also teach the A Level continuation, which matters because the habits that earn marks at 0478 are the ones a student carries into Year 12.

intro.heading: Why 0478 catches out students who can already program
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science, syllabus code 0478, is assessed by two written papers of equal weight. Paper 1 covers computer systems: data representation, data transmission, hardware, software, the internet and its uses, and automated and emerging technologies. Paper 2 covers algorithms, programming, databases and Boolean logic. There is no coursework component in the current syllabus, and no part of the qualification is marked at a computer. Every mark is earned in handwriting, under timing, against a mark scheme that expects particular words.

That last point explains most of the disappointment in this subject. Dubai has plenty of fifteen-year-olds who build things: a working Python game, a Discord bot, a tidy web project. Those students arrive in Year 11 confident and then score in the middle of Paper 2, because the paper does not ask them to make something work. It asks them to complete a trace table for somebody else's flawed algorithm, to write pseudocode in a syntax they have never used casually, and to explain in two marks' worth of words why a particular validation check is appropriate.

Paper 1 produces the opposite failure. Students treat it as general knowledge about computers, because much of it sounds familiar: RAM, routers, cloud storage, cyber security. The topics are then revised by reading rather than by answering, and the marks go missing in the detail. Describing how a packet is reassembled, converting between denary, binary and hexadecimal under pressure, or distinguishing a check digit from a checksum are all precise skills, and each one has a predictable set of wrong answers that a tutor has seen fifty times.

What a 0478 tutor does, then, is less about teaching programming than about converting knowledge into marks: writing pseudocode by hand to the conventions Cambridge uses, tracing code in a table without skipping iterations, converting number bases quickly and checking the answer, and answering a describe question with the number of distinct points the mark allocation implies. The content is usually already half there. The exam technique rarely is, and it is almost never taught in a class of twenty-six.

A note on how we deliver this in Dubai. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, on a fixed weekly slot in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses; in-home visits are a service we run only in India. For a programming subject, the shared screen is genuinely the better room: the tutor sees the student's actual code, runs it, breaks it deliberately, and annotates the pseudocode version alongside, with everything saved and sent afterwards. A visiting tutor leans over a laptop and leaves nothing behind for February revision.

Scarcity is the other reason online matching matters here. Computing specialists who teach both papers properly, including the database and Boolean logic topics that schools frequently reach in the final term, are a much smaller population than maths or English tutors. Within driving distance of any one Dubai community that population may be two or three people, none of them free at six in the evening. Across a national pool working over video it is a real choice, and the tutor can be matched to the programming language the school actually teaches rather than to the one they prefer.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-computer-science-0.programmesIntro: Computing sits in a vertical line from lower secondary to A Level, and the step between each stage is sharper than in most subjects. These are the stages a Dubai 0478 student is moving between, with what each transition actually requires.

programmes.name: Cambridge Lower Secondary Computing
programmes.description: Block-based and early text-based programming, basic networks and data concepts, taught in short weekly lessons. The stage builds confidence with a keyboard but very little of the formal precision that IGCSE assessment demands, which is why able Year 9 students can still find Year 10 abrupt.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai this stage is frequently taught as one lesson a week by a teacher who also covers ICT and design technology, so coverage varies between schools far more than in maths or science. Students arriving from other systems mid-secondary often have strong practical skills and no exposure to binary, logic gates or pseudocode conventions. A short diagnostic before Year 10 is cheap and prevents a term of guessing.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478
programmes.description: Two years ending in two written papers of equal weight. Paper 1 examines computer systems across six topics; Paper 2 examines algorithm design and problem-solving, programming, databases and Boolean logic. Candidates write pseudocode or a high-level language by hand, and no component is assessed at a computer.
programmes.countryNote: 0478 is a popular option block choice in Dubai's British-curriculum schools, which dominate private enrolment in the emirate. It frequently competes for timetable space with ICT 0417 and with a third science, and because KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the licensed curriculum, the option columns in Dubai schools are tighter than in the UK. Many students choose between computing subjects rather than taking both.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level Computer Science 9618
programmes.description: The post-16 continuation, with substantially more depth on data structures, logic, system software and a programming project at A Level. Students who reached a strong 0478 grade through memorised answers rather than understanding tend to stall in the first term of Year 12.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai students decide between A Level and the IB Diploma in the spring of Year 11. For computing, the practical implication is that 9618 assumes fluency in one text-based language, so a student who spent 0478 avoiding code is choosing a hard two years. Tutors working with Dubai families often use the summer between Year 11 and Year 12 to build that fluency properly, when there is time and no deadline.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Computer Science
programmes.description: The IB route, assessed through written papers and an internally assessed solution the student develops themselves. The emphasis on design documentation and on justifying choices is heavier than at IGCSE, and the internal assessment must be the candidate's own work throughout.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's IB sector is substantial and growing, with three new IB schools among the seven private schools opening for 2026-27. A 0478 student moving into IB Computer Science gains from the algorithmic foundation but has to learn a very different assessment culture, where a tutor's role is coaching and feedback on the student's own solution rather than any involvement in producing it.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-computer-science-0.subjectsIntro: These are the subjects that sit around 0478 on a Dubai timetable. The notes name what each one shares with computer science, because families deciding where to put tutoring hours need to know which problems overlap.

subjects.name: Computer Science (0478)
subjects.description: Computer systems in one paper, algorithms, programming, databases and Boolean logic in the other. Marks concentrate in precision: handwritten pseudocode, complete trace tables, base conversions and describe answers that hit the mark allocation.

subjects.name: Information and Communication Technology (0417)
subjects.description: Largely practical, with document production, databases, presentations, spreadsheets and website authoring assessed at a computer. Often confused with 0478 by parents; the two subjects share almost no assessment style.

subjects.name: Mathematics (0580)
subjects.description: The strongest predictor of comfort in Paper 2. Students fluent with algebraic manipulation and sequences handle iteration, counters and totalling far more easily than those still working arithmetic out step by step.

subjects.name: Cambridge International Mathematics (0607)
subjects.description: Taken instead of 0580 at some Dubai schools, with a stronger graphical calculator element. Useful for students heading to IB, and the problem-solving habits transfer directly into algorithm design.

subjects.name: Physics (0625)
subjects.description: Shares the discipline of describing a process in exactly the right terms for the marks available. Students who write loose physics explanations tend to write loose computing explanations too, and the fix is the same.

subjects.name: Chemistry (0620)

sections.heading: What the 0478 search is really asking
paragraphs: Parents typing for a Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 tutor in Dubai have usually just read a report or a mock result that does not match their sense of their child. The common version is a student who is visibly good with computers and who scored a grade 5. The less common version, and the harder one, is a student who revises diligently for the theory paper, remembers everything, and still drops a third of the available marks.

Both are exam-technique problems with content underneath. The first student knows how to make a program work and has never been taught that Paper 2 rewards a different thing: an algorithm expressed in a specific written form, traced correctly, with validation and error handling named rather than implied. The second student knows the content of Paper 1 and answers in the wrong grain, writing three sentences where the mark scheme wants two distinct technical points, or naming a technology without describing what it does.

A specialist tutor fixes those in a different order from a classroom teacher. The classroom has to cover the syllabus for everyone. A one-to-one tutor can start with the student's last script, identify the three habits costing the most, and spend a month on those while the class moves on. That is the whole value of one-to-one for this subject, and it is why a diagnostic matters more than a syllabus plan at the start.

The remainder of this page is the detail: what each paper examines, where the marks actually go, how pseudocode and trace tables are drilled, what the subject costs in this market, how Dubai option blocks and the permit rules work, and how the entry calendar constrains the year.

sections.heading: Paper 1: computer systems, topic by topic
paragraphs: Paper 1 covers six topics and carries half the qualification. The topics are data representation, data transmission, hardware, software, the internet and its uses, and automated and emerging technologies. Confirm the exact structure, duration and mark total against the Cambridge 0478 syllabus for your child's exam series, because these details are revised between syllabus cycles and a tutor working from an old specification is a real risk in this subject.

The pattern of lost marks is remarkably consistent across students and schools. Number bases are the first: converting between denary, binary and hexadecimal is examined every series, it is entirely mechanical, and students lose marks through arithmetic slips because they never learned to check the conversion backwards. Data transmission is the second: packet structure, serial and parallel, simplex and duplex, and the error-checking methods, where parity, checksum and check digit get blurred into one vague answer.

Hardware and software reward precision about purpose. A student who writes that RAM 'stores things the computer is using' has written something true and unmarkable. The paper wants the distinction between volatile and non-volatile, what the processor fetches and when, and what happens when physical memory runs short. Emerging technologies and the internet topics look like the easy marks and often are, provided the student can describe a mechanism rather than name a product.

The table below sets out the topics with what each one demands and where scripts usually leak marks. It is the version we work through in a first diagnostic session, scoring each row honestly, because a student who knows which two rows are weak can revise in a way that a student revising 'Paper 1' cannot.

sections.heading: Paper 2: algorithms, programming, databases and logic
paragraphs: Paper 2 carries the other half of the grade and is where most of the difference between a grade 6 and a grade 8 lives. It examines algorithm design and problem-solving, programming, databases and Boolean logic. Candidates write in pseudocode or a high-level programming language by hand. Cambridge publishes its own pseudocode conventions, and a student who writes Python syntax where pseudocode is expected can still be credited, but only if the logic is unambiguous, which casual code rarely is.

The questions have recognisable shapes. There is normally an algorithm to complete or correct; a trace table to fill from given code; a validation or verification check to write; a program to write to a short specification; a database question requiring field types, a primary key or a query; and Boolean logic in the form of a truth table, an expression or a logic circuit. Each shape has a method, and the method can be taught in an hour and then drilled.

The single biggest avoidable loss is the incomplete trace table. Students stop a row early, skip an iteration, or write only the final values rather than the changing ones, and the marks are awarded for the intermediate states. The second biggest is the unnamed variable: a student describes what their algorithm does without declaring or initialising anything, and the mark scheme has nothing to award against. The third is writing a working program that does not address the specification as written.

None of that requires more coding ability. It requires handwriting algorithms on paper under timing, which is the thing almost no student does voluntarily. We set it every week, because the exam is handwritten and typing practice does not transfer as cleanly as students assume.

sections.heading: The student who can code but cannot answer the question
paragraphs: This is the most common profile we see in Dubai, and it is worth describing precisely because the fix is specific. The student writes fluent Python. They debug by running the program and watching what happens. They have never designed an algorithm away from a machine, and they have never had to be right the first time without feedback from an interpreter.

Paper 2 removes the interpreter. There is no run button, no error message, no chance to try the other operator and see. Everything that the machine was doing for the student, they now have to do in their head and record on paper, which is exactly what a trace table is for. Students resist trace tables because they feel slow and clerical. They are slow and clerical, and they are also the mechanism by which a candidate verifies their own logic in an exam, and they carry marks in their own right.

The second half of the fix is the written register. Pseudocode in Cambridge's conventions is deliberately unambiguous: variables are declared, loops are closed explicitly, conditions are stated in full. Casual code is full of shortcuts that a machine tolerates and a mark scheme cannot read. We spend early sessions converting the student's own working program into clean handwritten pseudocode, which is a far better exercise than any set problem, because the student already knows the answer and is learning only the form.

Progress here is quick and visible. A student who could not complete a trace table in week one and can complete three accurately by week five has usually moved a grade on Paper 2, not because they understand programming better but because they have stopped losing marks they had already earned.

sections.heading: Databases and Boolean logic: the topics schools run out of time for
paragraphs: Two topics on Paper 2 are reliably underserved in school teaching, and both are cheap to fix. The first is the database topic, which examines single-table concepts: field types, primary keys, and a query that returns a specified set of records. Schools often arrive at it in the final term, teach it in two lessons, and move on. Students then treat a database table as a spreadsheet, choose a field type without thinking about what will be stored in it, and nominate a primary key that is not unique.

The second is Boolean logic. Truth tables, logic expressions and logic circuits are mechanical, learnable and worth real marks, and most students lose some of those marks through precedence errors with three inputs rather than through conceptual confusion. The reliable method is to build the truth table first, column by column for each gate, then read the expression or draw the circuit from the completed table rather than attempting it in one pass.

Both topics suit one-to-one work precisely because they are small and self-contained. A session and a half on databases and two sessions on logic will typically convert a vague performance into a reliable one, and unlike algorithm design they do not require weeks of habit change. For a Year 11 student six weeks from a paper, these are usually the highest-return hours available.

sections.heading: What a named-syllabus computing tutor costs in Dubai
paragraphs: Specialist computing tutors are scarcer than maths or English tutors in this market, and the rate reflects scarcity rather than difficulty. The figures below are published market rates in AED, each attributed to the provider or rate survey that published them in 2026. They are not IB Gram's price list and nothing here is a quote. We publish them because three of the six competitor pages reviewed for this market publish no price at all, and two quote in US dollars.

Two patterns are worth reading out of the table. The first is that in-home one-to-one carries a clear premium over online one-to-one, and that premium is travel time rather than better teaching; a tutor crossing Dubai for a 5pm lesson has lost ninety minutes of their day. The second is that small-group rates look attractive per student and work badly for this subject, because the gap between two students on Paper 2 is rarely the same gap, and a shared hour ends up covering theory that both already know.

There is also a scarcity effect specific to computing. A tutor who can teach both papers properly, including Boolean logic and database design, is a narrower population than a tutor who can help with Python homework. Families sometimes book the cheaper option and discover in February that the tutor was never going to cover the second half of Paper 2. The question to ask any prospective tutor is simple: walk me through how you teach trace tables.

IB Gram's model is a free first lesson with the matched specialist, no card details taken, then a written plan and a quote in AED once the tutor has seen a piece of the student's work. We publish the market bands so the quote arrives with context attached.

sections.heading: Option blocks, Dubai schools and who may legally tutor
paragraphs: Dubai's private school sector is the largest in the UAE, with 387,441 students across 227 schools offering 17 different curricula in 2024-25, and seven further private schools opening for 2026-27 that add 16,846 places. Enrolment grew six per cent during 2025-26. For a computing family, the practical consequence of that scale is choice between schools, and the practical constraint is what each school puts in its option columns.

KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students and specified instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit. Those requirements are legitimate and they consume timetable space, which is why Dubai option blocks are tighter than their UK equivalents and why 0478 and 0417 are frequently alternatives rather than companions. Ask the school which column computing sits in before Year 10 choices are made.

On the tutoring side, private tuition in the UAE is regulated. The private tuition work permit was introduced under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued by MoHRE free of charge for two years, and covers a defined set of eligible applicants. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted figure with suspicion. MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service is the official application route.

One ethical boundary applies across the Emirates. ADEK's professional-ethics rules bar Abu Dhabi school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit carries a code of conduct in the same spirit. An offer of your child's own class teacher, privately, should be declined. IB Gram holds no accreditation from KHDA, ADEK, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or any school, and operates no UAE office.

sections.heading: Series, entry deadlines and the zone timetable
paragraphs: Cambridge runs IGCSE examinations in a June series and a November series, and the deadlines that matter sit months before the papers. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series show the shape clearly: final entries close on 27 November 2026 for an exam period beginning on 3 February 2027, with forecast grades due on 27 February 2027 and results released on Direct on 13 May. Dates differ by series, but the lead time does not, and the deadline a family can actually miss is the school's internal one.

There is an administrative detail worth knowing. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a separate timetable version for each, stating that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam through using the wrong one. If your child is working from a timetable downloaded from a forum rather than the one the school issued, fix that today; it costs nothing and the downside is total.

Read backwards from the window, a 0478 year has a natural shape. All six Paper 1 topics covered by the end of term one of Year 11, with a scored diagnostic per topic. Trace tables and pseudocode practised weekly from the autumn rather than started in the spring, because they are habits rather than content. Databases and logic cleared by February. Full papers under timing from February, with the second half of each paper attempted first occasionally, since that is where fatigue costs marks.

For students taking Pearson Edexcel International GCSE subjects alongside Cambridge ones, the calendars differ: Pearson runs May or June and November series, with its November 2026 timetable running to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results issued to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students the following day, and November 2025 results reaching students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables that can be revised, so check the live official timetable rather than a restated date.
