sections.heading: Native speaker or trained teacher: which premium is worth paying?
paragraphs: Dubai's French tutoring market is full of native speakers, and families reasonably assume that fluency is the credential. For 0520 it is the weaker of the two credentials available, and understanding why saves real money.

Fluency lets somebody correct a sentence. Training lets them explain that your child keeps losing marks because the past participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is etre, and that the ear gives no warning because the ending is silent. It lets them know that the reading paper paraphrases systematically and that word-matching is the habit to break. It lets them mark against the published criteria rather than according to taste. A native speaker with a teaching qualification and experience of marking Cambridge scripts has both credentials and is worth a premium. A native speaker with neither is selling conversation practice, which is a genuine product at a much lower price and will not move a grade held down by accuracy.

There is a version of this that matters specifically in Dubai. A large number of students in this city have francophone family backgrounds, and parents in that position often hire a native speaker because the match feels natural. That is frequently the wrong purchase for exactly the student who needs it least: the heritage speaker's problem is written accuracy, and more conversation in French with a fluent adult is the one intervention guaranteed not to touch it. Ask any prospective tutor how many Cambridge French scripts they have marked and what they would do about participle agreement. The answer separates the two credentials in about fifteen seconds.

sections.heading: Scheduling against the Dubai school week, Ramadan and the exam term
paragraphs: A plan only works if the session happens, and in Dubai the predictable disruptions are known a year ahead. The school week ends on Friday for most British-curriculum schools, which makes Thursday evenings and weekend mornings unusually valuable slots, and makes Sunday the most commonly cancelled session of the week because of homework backlog.

The 16:30 slot is the one families want and the one that works least often. School buses in outlying communities arrive late, and a child who walks in at 16:20 is not ready to rehearse spoken French at 16:30. For most of the communities we teach in, 17:30 is the realistic earliest start on a school night, and two shorter sessions later in the evening produce a better trail of evidence than one long session that gets moved twice and then cancelled.

Ramadan is handled badly by most arrangements. Timetables compress, afternoons are tiring and the hours after Iftar are the sharpest of the day for many students. The straightforward fix is to move the slot rather than pause the cycle, keeping the fortnightly marked task on its schedule so the trend data survives the month. Short speaking drills suit a later slot particularly well. For the exam term, the fixed points are administrative rather than academic: Cambridge runs June and November series, and its published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries at 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027. Book the block in the term before, because the final weeks are when evening capacity in this city stops existing at any price.

sections.heading: If no 0520 specialist is free: the fallback, stated in advance
paragraphs: Every tutoring company in this market implies unlimited availability and none of them has it. We would rather publish the limit than discover it with you in week one, so here it is: Cambridge French specialists with a marking record are a finite group, the 16:30 to 19:30 Gulf Standard Time window is where every Dubai family wants to sit, and in the weeks before a series that window fills.

When a specialist is not available in your slot, there are three honest responses and we use them in this order. Move the slot: a 20:00 session or a weekend morning usually opens the choice back up immediately, and for speaking rehearsal a weekend slot is often better anyway. Change the format: two thirty-minute sessions can frequently be fitted where one sixty-minute block cannot. Or wait, with a date, rather than being handed a generalist and told they cover languages.

The one thing we will not do is place a tutor who has never marked a Cambridge French script and describe them as a 0520 specialist. If the only available person is a strong general French teacher without that specific experience, we say that explicitly, explain what they can and cannot do for your child's profile, and let you decide. A family whose problem is listening technique may be perfectly well served by that tutor; a family whose problem is participle agreement will not be. Disclosing which situation you are in costs us bookings and is the whole basis on which this page is worth reading.

sections.heading: Questions to ask before you pay any French tutor in Dubai
paragraphs: Most families ask about price and availability, which are the two least informative questions. A short list of better ones separates a syllabus teacher from a fluent speaker in a single phone call, and it works whichever format you choose.

Ask which board and syllabus code they teach, and listen for whether they distinguish Cambridge 0520 from the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE, which differ in component structure and in how speaking is conducted. Ask how many French scripts they have marked and what their marking looks like when it comes back. Ask what they would do about past participle agreement with a preceding direct object, which is a rule rarely taught properly and a fast test of depth. Ask whether speaking practice is recorded. Ask what arrives in writing after a session, and how often.

Then ask the two administrative questions almost nobody asks. Does the tutor hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, which is granted free of charge for two years and applied for through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service? And, if they are a registered school teacher, is your child enrolled at their school, because press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes staff being barred from paid private tutoring of their own school's students, and the permit's code of conduct is reported to bar serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. Verify the current wording with the relevant authority before relying on it, and treat a reluctance to discuss the permit as an answer in itself.

faqs.question: Do you provide a French 0520 home tutor who comes to our house in Dubai?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai or anywhere in the UAE, and in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not a service we sell; home visiting is offered only in India. Every 0520 session runs one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. We publish the in-home market rates and real drive times on this page anyway, so that if a genuinely strong Cambridge French teacher lives ten minutes from you, you can weigh that option against ours using numbers rather than claims.

faqs.question: How much more does in-home French tuition cost than online in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Roughly a third more at comparable quality, and the difference is transport rather than teaching. Bestimate's 2026 Dubai survey puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors quoting AED 200 to 500. Qualified subject teachers working online publish from about AED 150 to 300, and IGCSE or IB specialists AED 200 to 450 and above. Those are market figures read in October 2026, not our prices. Watch for minimum booking lengths too, since a quoted hourly rate on a compulsory two-hour visit is not comparable to a single online hour.

faqs.question: Does my child learn French better with a tutor physically in the room?
faqs.answer: For a language, usually not, and for two specific reasons. Speaking practice benefits enormously from being recorded and replayed, which is awkward in a living room and routine on video, and children consistently hear hesitations in playback that they never notice while talking. Written work on a shared document keeps its version history, so the same sentence can be shown rewritten three times across a month. Younger children who need supervision as much as teaching are the real exception, and we say so rather than pretending otherwise.

faqs.question: What does an in-home French tutor's drive actually cost us in lesson time?
faqs.answer: Often ten minutes of the hour and a great deal of flexibility. In dense apartment areas such as Discovery Gardens or Business Bay, visitor parking fills by early evening and building security plus lift waits sit inside the visit, so a tutor arriving at 17:45 for an 18:00 start is routine and the lesson quietly becomes fifty minutes. The larger cost is rigidity. A tutor with a fifty-minute commute cannot absorb a school revision session moving your child's availability by an hour; a video slot can move at short notice.

faqs.question: What should a French session leave behind for us to look at?
faqs.answer: Four things, every fortnight. A marked written task with errors grouped into named categories in English and a count beside each, so a parent who does not read French can see the pattern. A recorded speaking response with a time-to-first-word figure and a short pronunciation note. One stated priority for the coming fortnight. And a note of which error categories from the previous task have stopped appearing, which is where learning becomes visible. What should not be in the set is a predicted grade, because Cambridge sets boundaries after marking.

faqs.question: Which part of my child's French improves fastest with tutoring?
faqs.answer: Reading and listening technique, often within three or four sessions, because most lost marks there come from habits rather than from language. Written error categories move second, with a named rule usually stopping inside six weeks of marked tasks. Unrehearsed spoken fluency moves last and least, which is the opposite of what most families expect. A genuine comprehension gap from a missed year or a late start does not move in a term at all, and that is worth knowing in September rather than discovering in March.

faqs.question: Is a native French speaker worth paying more for at 0520?
faqs.answer: Only if they also have teaching training and a Cambridge marking record. Fluency lets somebody correct a sentence; training lets them explain that the past participle agrees with the subject when the auxiliary is etre and that the ear gives no warning because the ending is silent. For a heritage speaker whose grade is held down by written accuracy, more conversation with a fluent adult is the one intervention guaranteed not to help. Ask how many French scripts they have marked, and what they would do about participle agreement with a preceding direct object.

faqs.question: Can two siblings share one French session to halve the cost?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and only when the profiles genuinely overlap. Two children on the same syllabus, within about a year of each other, sharing the same weakness, can work productively together and split the cost. Two children at different levels, or one with a writing problem and one with a speaking problem, each receive half a lesson and neither problem gets solved. We will tell you which situation you are in before you book, decline the pairing where it will not work, and keep written tasks set and marked individually in any case.

faqs.question: What is the earliest realistic session time on a Dubai school night?
faqs.answer: For most of the communities we teach in, 17:30 rather than the 16:30 most families ask for. School buses in outlying areas arrive late, and a child who walks in at 16:20 is not ready to rehearse spoken French ten minutes later. Thursday evenings and weekend mornings are the most valuable slots because the British-curriculum school week ends on Friday, and Sunday sessions are the most frequently cancelled because of homework backlog. Two shorter sessions later in the evening usually survive the term better than one long early one.

faqs.question: How do French sessions work through Ramadan in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Move the slot rather than pausing the cycle. School timetables compress, afternoons are tiring and the hours after Iftar are the sharpest of the day for many students, so a post-Iftar session for the month keeps the fortnightly marked task on schedule and preserves the trend data that a pause destroys. Short speaking drills suit a later, shorter slot particularly well. There is no travel penalty on a moved session, because there is no car journey anyone needs compensating for.

faqs.question: What happens if no Cambridge French specialist is free in our slot?
faqs.answer: We tell you, and we offer three things in order. Move the slot, since a 20:00 session or a weekend morning usually opens the choice immediately and suits speaking rehearsal anyway. Change the format, because two thirty-minute sessions often fit where one sixty-minute block cannot. Or wait, with a date attached. What we will not do is place a tutor with no Cambridge French marking record and describe them as a 0520 specialist. If that is the only option, we say so and explain what they can and cannot do for your child's profile.

faqs.question: Should we use the school's French clinic instead of paying a tutor?
faqs.answer: Try it first, because most Dubai French departments run a lunchtime or after-school clinic and a surprising number of students have never attended one. For vocabulary gaps and homework questions it is free and genuinely useful. What it rarely provides is individual marked written work with errors grouped by rule, or recorded one-to-one speaking rehearsal, because neither is possible with a group. A reasonable arrangement for a tight budget is the school clinic for vocabulary plus a fortnightly marked-task session, which costs far less than a weekly hour.

faqs.question: Does the tutor need a MoHRE permit, and can we ask to see it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should ask. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, with applications made through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service via its smart app, website or e-services system. Individuals tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule has been published so no amount should be quoted to you. Reluctance to discuss the permit is an answer in itself.

faqs.question: Can we book a French block for the weeks right before the exam?
faqs.answer: Book it in the preceding term, not in the final six weeks. Published hourly rates mostly hold steady as a series approaches; what disappears is capacity in the 16:30 to 19:30 window, which is where every Dubai family wants to sit. A block agreed a term ahead costs the same per hour and actually exists. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries at 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, which shows how early the administrative decisions really sit.

faqs.question: How do we tell after a term whether the French tutoring was worth the money?
faqs.answer: By counting artefacts rather than recalling impressions. A term of fortnightly marking should have produced about six marked scripts; three are noise, six are arguable, ten are defensible. Look for error categories that have stopped appearing rather than for a rising mark, since task difficulty moves single marks around. Look at the time-to-first-word figures on the speaking recordings. And look at the six-session written reviews, because a review process that can only ever say continue is not a review process at all.

intro.heading: The mechanics of teaching French 0520 over live video
paragraphs: Online tuition is normally argued for on logistics: no traffic, no parking, no evening lost to Sheikh Zayed Road. Those things are true and they are the least interesting part of the case. The substantive argument is that a video session can do four things a living room cannot do easily at all, and all four of them happen to be the things Cambridge IGCSE French actually rewards.

The first is audio control. The listening component is the paper where Dubai students lose the most marks to technique rather than language, and practising it properly means playing a file at exactly the right volume, stopping at a precise second, replaying one sentence twenty times and then analysing why the negative was missed. A tutor sharing their own audio output does all of that in a click. A tutor at a kitchen table holding a phone speaker near a notebook is approximating it badly, and nobody admits that out loud.

The second is the record button. Spoken French improves when a student hears themselves, not when they are told how they sounded. A recorded response, replayed in the same session with the tutor silent, produces a reaction no amount of feedback achieves: the four-second silence before a simple answer is suddenly audible, the fillers are countable, the nasal vowel that flattened is obvious. Recording in a private home with a visiting adult is socially awkward and technically fiddly; recording in a video session is a default setting, taken with the family's explicit consent and deletable on request.

The third is the shared document. French is a language where meaning lives in marks that are easy to lose by hand: the grave accent that separates a verb form from a preposition, the acute that changes a participle, the cedilla that keeps a consonant soft. On a shared screen a tutor can zoom, colour and label those marks, and the version history keeps every earlier draft, so a parent can be shown the same sentence rewritten three times across a month. A notebook keeps only the final version, which is the least informative one. The fourth is the pool: the tutor is chosen on marking record rather than on willingness to drive to your community at 17:00.

IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai, and in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not a service we sell in any emirate; home visiting is offered only in India. What follows is not a defence of that position but a description of how the sessions actually run, written in enough detail that you can judge whether the format suits your child, and spot a provider who has simply moved a classroom habit onto a webcam.

regions.name: Dubai Production City and Arjan
regions.note: Apartment living with long single approach roads and late bus returns. An 18:00 start is the realistic one, and the twice-weekly thirty-minute speaking format works far better here than a single long evening session.

regions.name: Jumeirah Islands and The Lakes
regions.note: Quiet villa communities with early school returns, which makes the 16:30 slot genuinely usable. Worth taking, because retrieval drills work better before a child is tired than after supper.

regions.name: International City and Warsan
regions.note: Dense, mixed-curriculum housing where many students take French as a third language alongside Arabic and English. Vocabulary load is the binding constraint, so spaced retrieval matters more than lesson length.

regions.name: Al Mizhar, Al Twar and Al Qusais
regions.note: Established northern districts with short school runs. Families here often have siblings on different syllabuses and benefit from staggered short sessions rather than one shared hour.

regions.name: Dubai Investment Park and Green Community
regions.note: Long commutes to the main school clusters mean children arrive home late and tired. Weekend morning sessions are unusually productive in this part of the city and are easy to schedule when no one is driving.

regions.name: Tilal Al Ghaf and Damac Hills
regions.note: Newer communities with a fast-growing school presence and almost no resident tutoring supply. This is where removing the drive radius changes the available choice of French teacher most dramatically.

regions.name: Al Jaddaf and Za'abeel
regions.note: Central apartment living with reliable connectivity and compact study spaces. A headset and a shared screen are more practical here than a table covered in textbooks, which suits the format well.

schoolClusters.city: Al Barsha South, Arjan and Dubai Hills
schoolClusters.note: A cluster of newer British-curriculum and international schools with large year groups and wide-ability French sets. Enquiries here are dominated by Year 10 students sitting in the top set and performing near the bottom of it, which is nearly always a precision problem rather than a comprehension one.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-french-0520-online.modesIntro: Three formats that only really work over video, chosen by what the diagnosis says has to move. None of them is a shortened version of a classroom lesson.

modes.title: Split-screen paper clinic
modes.description: A past paper on one side of the screen, the mark scheme logic on the other, and the tutor annotating in real time as the student works. The point is that the student sees their own reasoning being diagnosed rather than hearing a correction afterwards. Timed sets, with every missed item logged by cause rather than counted.

modes.title: Spaced retrieval micro-sessions
modes.description: Two or three short sessions a week rather than one long one, built around retrieval at increasing intervals. Vocabulary and verb forms are held by frequency rather than by duration, and a twenty-five minute slot costs less per week than an hour while producing more. This is the format a commuting tutor cannot offer at any price.

modes.title: Recorded speaking rehearsal
modes.description: Unseen prompts, timed responses, recorded with consent, then played back with the tutor silent. Unprompted turns are measured in seconds and logged. Students change their preparation habits the first time they hear their own hesitation, which is a thing that happens once and then does not need repeating.

sections.heading: A sixty-minute online French session, minute by minute
paragraphs: The question families most want answered about online tuition is the most concrete one: what actually happens for an hour. A session that is a video call with a conversation in it has wasted the format, and a great many of them are exactly that. The shape below is what a 0520 session looks like when the tools are being used for something.

It opens with retrieval rather than greeting. Five minutes of rapid recall on items from previous sessions, resurfaced at widening intervals, with the student answering aloud and the tutor logging what did not come back. Then the component of the week: either a timed paper section with the audio shared from the source file, or a written task taken apart error category by error category, or recorded speaking rehearsal on unseen prompts. One component, not four, because a session that touches everything achieves nothing in particular.

It closes with two things that outlive the hour. The next fortnight's priority, stated in one line and typed into the shared document where the student can see it. And the artefact: an annotated paper, a marked task, or a recorded file, saved to the folder the family can open. The last ninety seconds are spent confirming the homework, which for a language is almost always short and frequent rather than long and weekly. A session that ends with the tutor saying goodbye and nothing being saved has produced a pleasant hour and no evidence.

sections.heading: Delivering the listening paper's audio properly
paragraphs: The listening component is where Dubai students lose the most marks for reasons that are not about French, and it is also the component most badly served by well-meaning tutoring of any format. Playing French audio in the background does nothing. Playing a track once, asking how it went, and moving on does very little. The work is answering items, marking them, and then classifying every miss by cause.

Three causes account for most of it. Negation, where a speaker says they no longer do something and the student answers the first half of the sentence, made worse in French because the negative wraps the verb and the second element can land several words later. Numbers, times and prices, which are the cheapest marks on the paper and the most frequently dropped, because French numbers above sixty are constructed rather than named and dates arrive in an order British-curriculum students do not expect. And the rejected distractor, where an option is mentioned and then dismissed, and the student selects it because it was in the recording.

Fixing those requires precision replay, and precision replay is where the format decides the quality. A tutor sharing their own audio output can stop on a syllable, loop one clause fifteen times, drop the speed, and show the student exactly where attention failed. The same tutor in a living room is holding a phone near a child's ear and guessing. We log every missed item by cause rather than by number, because three marks lost to negation and three lost to numbers are two different problems needing two different drills, and a score out of twenty tells you which neither of them is.
bullets: Audio shared from the source, looped and slowed on demand
Every missed item classified: negation, number, distractor or timing
Negation drilled as a trigger for attention rather than as a grammar rule
Numbers, times and prices practised as sounds, not as written forms

sections.heading: Speaking over video: latency, overlap and the record button
paragraphs: The honest objection to teaching speaking over video is latency. A call adds a fraction of a second in each direction, which makes natural overlap awkward and can make a student hesitate for a reason that has nothing to do with their French. Any provider claiming the format has no downside here is not paying attention. The answer is to design around it rather than deny it.

In practice that means three adjustments. Turn-taking is made explicit at the start, so a pause is understood as the connection rather than as disapproval. Interruption is used deliberately and sparingly, because talking over a student on a call is far more disruptive than in a room. And the parts of the speaking test that depend on rapid back-and-forth are rehearsed with a deliberately brisk tutor, so that the real test, conducted in person at the school with no latency at all, feels easier rather than harder. Students consistently report the live test as less pressured than the rehearsal, which is the right direction for that surprise to run.

Against that one real cost sits the record button, which is worth considerably more. A recorded response played back with the tutor silent produces the single most useful moment in language teaching: the student hears their own four-second silence before a simple answer, counts their own fillers, and notices the nasal vowel that flattened. Being told those things changes very little. Hearing them changes preparation habits immediately. Recording happens only with the family's explicit consent, the files belong to the family, and they are deleted on request; session records involving minors deserve that care under the UAE's personal data framework rather than a line in a terms page.

sections.heading: The shared document: accents, drafts and the dead-end correction
paragraphs: French accuracy lives in small marks. A grave accent separates a verb form from a preposition. An acute changes a participle. A cedilla keeps a consonant soft. Students lose marks on these constantly, and the loss is invisible to the ear because none of them is pronounced as a separate sound, which is why spoken practice never surfaces them.

A shared document fixes two problems at once. The tutor can zoom in, colour the mark, and label what it does, which is a different experience from a circle in a margin. And the version history keeps every draft, so the tutor can show a parent the same sentence as it was written in September, in October and in November. That progression is the clearest evidence of learning that exists in a language, and a notebook preserves only the final version, which is the least informative one. We also use it to enforce a rule about marking: the rewritten sentence is always typed by the student, never by the tutor.

That rule exists for an academic-honesty reason as well as a pedagogical one. A tutor may teach, model, question, mark and give feedback. A tutor may not supply sentences for submission or improve a piece of assessed work to the point where the French is no longer the student's own. The practical test we apply is whether the student can produce the corrected version unaided; if they cannot, the correction was pitched at the wrong level and the teaching needs changing rather than the script. A document with full version history makes that boundary visible rather than a matter of trust, which protects the student far more than it inconveniences us.

sections.heading: Where your tutor is, and why we tell you
paragraphs: Several companies serving UAE parents route enquiries to numbers outside the country and never say where the teaching happens. We state the tutor's base because a family paying for their child's French is entitled to know who is in the room, even when the room is a screen.

The practical issues are timezone and school calendar, not nationality. A tutor in Europe is three or four hours behind Gulf Standard Time depending on the season, which makes a Dubai 17:30 slot a comfortable early afternoon for them and a Dubai 20:00 slot straightforward. It also means their own holiday pattern differs from the Dubai school year, which has to be planned rather than discovered. A tutor in the UAE shares your calendar and your Ramadan schedule, which is genuinely easier, and is drawn from a smaller pool.

What we will not do is use a non-UAE contact route as the conversion path while implying a local presence, or state a Dubai address we do not occupy. IB Gram operates no premises in the UAE, holds no KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, and claims no approval, accreditation or endorsement from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, Cambridge or Pearson. Those bodies are described on this page because their rules affect your decisions, not because any of them has anything to do with us. Any tutoring company in this market implying otherwise is making a claim worth asking about directly.

sections.heading: Technology, bandwidth and what we ask of a Dubai household
paragraphs: The setup requirements are modest and worth stating precisely, because the commonest cause of a bad online language lesson is not the internet but the audio. A laptop or tablet rather than a phone, because the shared document has to be legible. Wired headphones with a microphone rather than the device speakers, because open speakers cause echo and echo destroys listening practice specifically. A quiet corner, which in an apartment usually means a bedroom rather than a living room.

Bandwidth is rarely the problem in Dubai. What does cause trouble is a household on a single connection with three children streaming at 18:00, and the fix is a schedule rather than an upgrade. We ask families to test the setup during the free diagnostic rather than on the first paid session, which sounds obvious and is routinely skipped. A five-minute check before anybody pays prevents the most common first-session failure.

Two things deserve more care than a checklist. Recording is taken only with explicit consent, and we state what is kept, why, and how to have it deleted. Lead forms collect personal information about a minor, so they should say what is collected and why, keep a privacy link visible, and never ask for a child's school, grades and photograph without a stated purpose; the UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on personal data protection is the reason this matters rather than a formality. If a provider cannot tell you where a recording of your child is stored, that is a reason to ask more questions before the second session.

sections.heading: What online teaching cannot fix
paragraphs: A page arguing for a format should be honest about its limits, and there are three real ones. The first is supervision. A nine or ten year old who will not sit still without an adult present is not well served by a video session, and neither is a teenager who closes the window the moment nobody is watching. That is a household problem rather than a teaching one, and an in-home tutor genuinely solves it. We say so rather than selling around it.

The second is a genuine comprehension gap. A student who has missed a year of French through a school move, or who started the language late, needs reading mileage and vocabulary breadth over two or three terms. No format accelerates that, no block of sessions compresses it, and a provider promising a transformation before a June series is not being straight with you. What the format does offer is frequency: short retrieval sessions three times a week are the single best treatment for that profile and are logistically impossible with a commuting tutor.

The third is the handwriting itself. Cambridge papers are handwritten, and a student who has composed exclusively on a keyboard for a year will be slower and messier under exam conditions. We set written work on paper, photographed and uploaded, for exactly that reason, and we time it. A provider whose written practice happens entirely in a text box has quietly removed a skill the exam tests. None of these three limits is a reason to choose a worse teacher who lives nearby; they are reasons to design the arrangement knowingly.

sections.heading: The folder a parent can audit after twelve weeks
paragraphs: Everything above exists to produce one thing: a set of documents a parent who does not read French can open at the end of a term and draw a conclusion from. Most tutoring in this city produces nothing of the kind, which is why the question of whether it worked usually gets answered with a feeling.

After twelve weeks the folder should contain roughly six marked written tasks, each with errors grouped into named categories in English and a count beside each; a set of recorded speaking files with time-to-first-word figures attached; a set of annotated papers with every missed item classified by cause; a running vocabulary list of the words that cost time in timed reading; and two written reviews, one at session six and one at session twelve, each carrying one of four verdicts. Three marked scripts are noise, six are arguable, ten are defensible, which is why the cycle is fortnightly rather than monthly.

The verdicts matter more than the documents. Continue, if the pattern is normal for the stage. Change the focus, if the figures show the original diagnosis was partly wrong, which most often means a presumed grammar problem is really a vocabulary problem. Change the tutor, if the chart is flat and the student has stopped volunteering, which is a fit issue and ours to fix; handovers are not charged for. Or stop, if the honest reading is that the school is doing the necessary work or another subject has a stronger claim on the budget. A review process that can only say continue is not a review process, and no document in that folder will ever contain a predicted grade, because Cambridge sets boundaries after marking and nobody else gets to.

faqs.question: How is the listening audio handled in an online 0520 lesson?
faqs.answer: Shared from the source file through the call, which is the main technical reason the format suits this component. A tutor can stop on a syllable, loop one clause fifteen times, slow the speed and show the student exactly where attention failed. Every missed item is then classified by cause rather than counted: negation, a misheard number, a mentioned-then-rejected distractor, or simply running out of time. A score out of twenty tells you which of those four it was not. That classification is what turns listening practice into teaching.

faqs.question: Can speaking really be taught properly over a video call?
faqs.answer: Yes, with one honest caveat. A call adds a fraction of a second each way, which makes natural overlap awkward, so turn-taking is made explicit and brisk rehearsal is used deliberately so the real test feels easier than the practice. Against that sits the record button, which is worth far more: a response played back with the tutor silent lets a student hear their own four-second silence, count their own fillers and notice a flattened nasal vowel. Being told those things changes little; hearing them changes preparation immediately.

faqs.question: Will my child's French speaking practice be recorded, and who keeps the files?
faqs.answer: Only with your explicit written consent, and the files belong to you. We state what is kept, why, and how to have it deleted, and we delete on request. Each recording comes with a time-to-first-word figure and a short dated pronunciation note covering nasal vowels, liaison and final consonants rather than general comments about fluency. The UAE's Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on personal data protection is the reason we treat session records about a minor carefully, not a line in a terms page nobody reads.

faqs.question: What equipment does an online French session actually need?
faqs.answer: Less than families expect, and the audio matters more than the internet. A laptop or tablet rather than a phone, so the shared document and annotated papers are legible. Wired headphones with a microphone rather than device speakers, because open speakers cause echo and echo specifically ruins precision listening work. A quiet corner, which in a Dubai apartment usually means a bedroom. Test all of it during the free diagnostic rather than on the first paid session; echo is the commonest cause of a disappointing first lesson and takes five minutes to rule out.

faqs.question: Does bandwidth in Dubai cause problems for live lessons?
faqs.answer: Rarely on its own. What causes trouble is a household on one connection with three children streaming at 18:00, and the answer is a schedule rather than a faster package. Communities with long bus journeys, such as Dubailand or Dubai Investment Park, hit a different constraint: children arrive home late and tired, so an 18:00 start and two shorter sessions a week survive the term better than one long early session. Weekend mornings are unusually productive in those areas and are trivially easy to schedule when nobody is driving.

faqs.question: Is my child's French tutor based in Dubai or somewhere else?
faqs.answer: We tell you before you book, because you are entitled to know. A tutor in Europe sits three or four hours behind Gulf Standard Time depending on the season, which makes a Dubai 17:30 or 20:00 slot straightforward, and keeps a holiday pattern different from the Dubai school year that has to be planned rather than discovered. A UAE-based tutor shares your calendar and Ramadan schedule and comes from a smaller pool. What we will not do is route you abroad while implying a local office, because IB Gram occupies no premises in the UAE.

faqs.question: How does written French work if everything is typed on a screen?
faqs.answer: It is not all typed. Cambridge papers are handwritten, so a student who composes exclusively on a keyboard for a year will be slower and messier under exam conditions. We set written work on paper, timed, photographed and uploaded, for exactly that reason. The shared document is used for analysis rather than for production: accents zoomed in on, coloured and labelled, with version history keeping every draft so the same sentence can be shown as it was written in September, October and November.

faqs.question: What does the version history in the shared document actually prove?
faqs.answer: That learning was retained rather than corrected once. A notebook keeps only the final version of a sentence, which is the least informative one. A document that holds three dated drafts of the same piece of writing shows a parent exactly which rule stopped being broken and when. It also makes an academic-honesty boundary visible rather than a matter of trust: the rewrite is always typed by the student, never by the tutor, and the record shows it. That protects your child far more than it inconveniences us.

faqs.question: Can an online tutor help with the French my child submits to school?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach, model, question, mark and give feedback. A tutor cannot supply sentences for submission or polish a piece of assessed work until the French is no longer the student's own. The working test is whether the student can produce the corrected version unaided; if not, the correction was pitched at the wrong level and the teaching needs changing rather than the script. We never type into a submission, and the shared document's history is the evidence of that rather than a promise about it.

faqs.question: Is online tutoring suitable for a younger child who needs supervising?
faqs.answer: Often not, and we would rather say so. A nine or ten year old who will not sit still without an adult present is poorly served by a video session, and so is a teenager who closes the window the moment nobody is watching. That is a household problem rather than a teaching one, and a tutor physically present genuinely solves it. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai and cannot offer that, so for families in that position the honest recommendation is to look locally, with the caveat that a weaker teacher nearby is still a weaker teacher.

faqs.question: How many short sessions a week are better than one long French lesson?
faqs.answer: Two or three of twenty-five minutes, for vocabulary, verb forms and speaking fluency. All three are held by frequency rather than by duration, and spaced retrieval at widening intervals outperforms a single weekly revisit by a wide margin. The format also costs less per week in the Dubai market than a full hour. Written accuracy work is the exception: marking and rewriting a task needs a longer block. A sensible shape for many students is one full session a fortnight plus two short retrieval slots a week.

faqs.question: Can we keep French lessons going if we leave Dubai mid-syllabus?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is the situation where the format earns its keep most clearly. A student leaving in March of Year 10 and arriving somewhere new in September has a six-month hole in a two-year course, and video teaching is the only arrangement that survives the move without restarting the relationship. The evidence folder travels too, so a new school can be shown a documented French profile with marked scripts and recorded speaking rather than a verbal account, which shortens the setting process noticeably.

faqs.question: Can my child take Cambridge French as a private candidate from Dubai?
faqs.answer: Yes, through a centre that accepts private candidates, and several Dubai centres do. Entry fees and deadlines are set by the centre rather than by any tutor, and the entry closes months before the papers, so contact centres early. A private candidate has nobody inside a school tracking that deadline on their behalf, which is the single most common way this route goes wrong. Teaching has to come entirely from outside the school in any case, which makes imposing a drive radius on yourself a strange constraint to accept.

intro.heading: What Cambridge IGCSE French 0520 actually tests, and why competent students still drop grades
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE French under syllabus code 0520 is a four-skill qualification. Listening, reading, speaking and writing are assessed as separate components, and on the current syllabus they carry equal weight. Confirm the exact weighting, component numbering and timings for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org, because Cambridge revises these by cohort and a figure read from a blog can be two syllabus versions out of date. The structural consequence of equal weighting is the thing most families miss: a student who is genuinely good at French and bad at one skill loses a quarter of the available marks, and no amount of extra vocabulary fixes that.

Every task on the paper is drawn from five broad topic areas: everyday activities, personal and social life, the world around us, the world of work, and the international world. Those areas are not a syllabus of facts to memorise. They are the territory from which an examiner will ask something unfamiliar, which is why vocabulary learned as lists performs so much worse than vocabulary learned in collocations. A student who knows that stage means a work placement rather than a platform has learned the word properly; a student who has it on a list under the heading of work has not.

Dubai adds a specific pattern to this. French in a British-curriculum Dubai school is usually taught in large sets with limited contact time, and the student population is unusually mixed: children who have genuinely lived in France, children from francophone African and Levantine backgrounds with strong spoken French and almost no written accuracy, and children who started French in Year 7 and have never heard it outside a classroom. Those three profiles fail 0520 in completely different ways, and a tutor who treats them identically will waste a term on the wrong skill.

The profile that surprises families most is the confident speaker. A child who sounds impressive in conversation, grew up around French, and reads well can still drop to a middling grade because written accuracy is assessed on things fluent speakers never attend to: whether the past participle agrees, whether the partitive article survives a negative, whether an accent that changes meaning is actually there. Spoken French forgives all of that. A Cambridge writing task does not. The reverse profile, the diligent Year 7 starter, usually writes accurately and freezes in the speaking test.

The rest of this page goes through the four components one at a time, names the failures that recur in each, and sets out what a session should actually do about them. There is no promised grade here and no claim about outcomes. What there is instead is a diagnosis you can apply before you hire anyone, including us, and enough detail to ask a prospective tutor a question they cannot answer with enthusiasm alone.

Five Cambridge topic areas from which every unfamiliar task is drawn
Three distinct Dubai student profiles that fail 0520 in different ways
Named grammar failures: auxiliary choice, participle agreement, partitive after negation

dubai/cambridge-igcse-french-0520-tutor.programmesIntro: French runs continuously from Year 7 to Year 13 in most Dubai British-curriculum schools, with a decision point at 16 that families rarely plan for. These are the four stages, described by what each one assesses rather than by what it is called.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE French (Foreign Language)
programmes.description: Four separately assessed skills drawn from five topic areas, graded on the Cambridge A* to G scale. The mechanical demands are modest; the accuracy demands are not. Most of the grade difference between a 6 and an 8 in this subject sits in participle agreement, tense selection and precision of vocabulary rather than in range.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai centres enter 0520 in both the June and November series, and the entry decision is made by the exams officer months before the papers. Ask which of Cambridge's six administrative zones your centre belongs to, because Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone and cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who uses the wrong one.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 and Cambridge Lower Secondary French
programmes.description: The years in which tense formation either becomes automatic or becomes a permanent weakness. Three tenses handled securely at the end of Year 9 is worth more at 0520 than six tenses half-known. Support at this stage is short, cheap and unglamorous: verb drilling, gender habits and reading aloud for pronunciation.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai timetables usually give French two or three periods a week against competing demands from mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies, which are required in all Dubai private schools whatever curriculum the school is licensed to teach. French therefore gets less contact time here than in a UK comprehensive, and the gap shows up in Year 10.

programmes.name: IB Diploma French B and French ab initio
programmes.description: The route for the large number of Dubai students who move from a British Year 11 into an IB Diploma school. A solid 0520 grade usually places a student into French B rather than ab initio, and the step up is in receptive demand and in the assessment of intercultural understanding rather than in grammar.
programmes.countryNote: Because Dubai has both British and IB schools in the same neighbourhoods, a student finishing 0520 here genuinely chooses between A Level French and IB French B. The deciding evidence is usually the speaking component: students who performed well under the 0520 speaking format tend to cope better with the IB individual oral.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS and A Level French
programmes.description: The continuation inside the Cambridge system, moving from topic-based tasks to literature or texts and to extended written argument. The jump that catches students is not vocabulary but register: writing an argued response in French is a different skill from writing a well-controlled description.
programmes.countryNote: Confirm the current component codes with your school's exams officer before planning, since Cambridge offers more than one French qualification at this level and Dubai centres differ in what they enter. A student with a strong 0520 writing profile and a weak speaking profile should know that before choosing a sixth-form route.

sections.heading: The four 0520 components, and what each one is really testing
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE French 0520 assesses listening, reading, speaking and writing as four separate components, equally weighted on the current syllabus. Confirm the current structure, timings and mark totals for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org before building a plan around them. The architecture matters more than the detail: because the weighting is even, the fastest route to a better grade is almost always to fix the weakest skill rather than to improve the strongest one.

The two receptive papers reward technique heavily. A listening item is rarely difficult French; it is a short piece of plausible speech containing a negative, a number, or a detail that is mentioned and then contradicted. A reading item rarely turns on an unknown word; it turns on whether the student can recognise that the text says the same thing as the question in different words. Students who revise for these papers by learning vocabulary improve slowly. Students who practise the specific traps improve quickly, because the trap inventory is small and repeatable.

The two productive components behave in the opposite way. Speaking and writing cannot be fixed by technique alone, because they expose whether the grammar is actually automatic. A student who can explain the rule for past participle agreement and still gets it wrong under time pressure has knowledge without automaticity, and the only cure is repetition on real tasks with marking. That difference, technique for the receptive skills and automaticity for the productive ones, is the single most useful thing a family can understand before buying any tuition at all.

sections.heading: The listening paper: three failures that account for most dropped marks
paragraphs: The first is negation. A speaker says they used to go to the gym but no longer do, or that the museum is open every day except Monday, and the student answers the first half of the sentence. French compounds this because the negative wraps around the verb and the second element can arrive several words after the first, so a student listening for content words rather than structure hears the affirmative and stops. The fix is mechanical: dozens of short items where the correct answer depends on a ne, a plus, a jamais or a sauf, until the pattern triggers attention automatically.

The second is quantity and number. Prices, times, dates, ages and quantities are the easiest marks on the paper and the most frequently lost, because French numbers between sixty and a hundred are constructed rather than named, and because dates are spoken in an order British-curriculum students do not expect. A student who has never drilled seventy-eight, ninety-two and quarter past as sounds rather than as written forms will lose two or three marks on a paper where every mark is proportionally expensive.

The third is the rejected distractor. A speaker mentions an option and then dismisses it: they considered taking the train, but in the end drove. The train is in the recording, the train is in the answer options, and a student under pressure selects it. This one is not a language failure at all; it is a reading of intent, and it is why practising listening by playing French audio in the background does nothing. Items have to be answered, marked, and then analysed by cause. We keep a log of every missed item by cause rather than by number, because three marks lost to negation and three lost to numbers are two different problems with two different cures.
bullets: Negation drilled as a trigger for attention, not as a grammar rule
Numbers, times, prices and dates practised as sounds
The mentioned-then-rejected option as a recognised pattern
Every missed item logged by cause rather than totalled

sections.heading: The reading paper: paraphrase, not word-spotting
paragraphs: The reading component punishes a habit that has worked for students all the way through Key Stage 3. In lower school, the answer to a comprehension question usually contains the same words as the question, so the technique of scanning for the matching word produces correct answers and gets rewarded. At 0520 the examiner systematically paraphrases, and the technique starts producing confident wrong answers instead.

Retraining this takes a specific exercise rather than more reading. We take a question, cover the text, and ask the student to list three different ways the same idea could be expressed in French before looking. That builds the habit of searching for meaning rather than form. It also exposes vocabulary gaps precisely where they matter, which is in the student's ability to recognise a synonym rather than to produce one. Recognition and production are different sizes of vocabulary, and the reading paper only needs the first.

Timing is the second half of the problem. Students who read every text fully before looking at the questions run out of time on the last section, which is typically where the harder items sit, and lose marks on questions they could have answered. The alternative order, questions first and targeted reading second, feels wrong to students taught to read carefully and works considerably better under exam conditions. Both the paraphrase exercise and the order change are improvements in technique that cost two or three sessions and are available to every student regardless of their level of French, which makes them the cheapest marks on this syllabus.

sections.heading: The speaking test, element by element
paragraphs: Speaking is the component Dubai students are least prepared for and the one families most often ignore until the term of the exam. The reason is practical: it is the only part of the syllabus that cannot be practised alone, in silence, from a textbook, and in a French set of twenty-eight students the amount of individual speaking time available in a week is very small.

On the current syllabus the test combines short role-play tasks with a presentation or discussion of a prepared topic and a general conversation across the syllabus topic areas. Confirm the exact format and timings for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org. The structural point that survives any revision is that part of the test is predictable and part of it is not, and students prepare only for the predictable part. A memorised topic presentation delivered fluently, followed by a general conversation in which the student cannot answer an unexpected question about their town, is the single most common speaking profile we meet.

Rehearsal has to be designed to break the script. We record with consent, ask follow-up questions the student has not seen, and then play back the moment where fluency collapsed. Students who hear their own four-second silence before a basic answer change their preparation habits immediately in a way that no amount of advice achieves. The measurable targets are time to first response and length of unprompted turn, both audible on a recording and both improvable within a term. Pronunciation gets its own log, focused on nasal vowels, liaison and the silent final consonants that make a correct word unrecognisable to an examiner.

sections.heading: Writing: the grammar that costs the most marks at 0520
paragraphs: Written French at IGCSE is marked on control rather than ambition. A short, accurate, well-connected answer scores better than a longer one reaching for structures the student cannot land. That single piece of information changes behaviour in one session, because most students are trying to impress rather than trying to be right.

The error profile is remarkably consistent across Dubai students. Auxiliary choice in the perfect tense comes first: which verbs take etre, and the agreement of the past participle with the subject when they do. Agreement of the past participle with a preceding direct object comes next and is rarely taught properly at all. Then the imperfect against the perfect, where students use whichever they learned most recently rather than distinguishing description and habit from completed action. Then the partitive, which collapses to de after a negative and after expressions of quantity. Then adjective agreement and position. Then accents that change meaning, where a missing grave on ou or a changes the word.

The teaching approach that works is narrow and repetitive, not comprehensive. One named rule per fortnight, practised on short tasks, marked by error category with a count, until that category stops appearing in the marking. Three cleared categories in a term is a realistic target and usually produces a visible change in the mark. A student who has had every error circled in red on four consecutive pieces has learned nothing in particular, which is the most common outcome of well-intentioned marking. The rewritten version is always produced by the student, never by the tutor: a correction the student cannot apply unaided was pitched at the wrong level.

sections.heading: The three Dubai student profiles, and what each one actually needs
paragraphs: A French set in a Dubai school contains students whose relationship with the language is radically different, and the single biggest waste of tutoring money in this subject is treating them the same. Three profiles cover almost all of the briefs we receive.

The first is the confident heritage or near-native speaker. Strong spoken French from family or from early schooling, good listening comprehension, and a written profile full of silent-ending errors. This student does not need conversation practice; buying it is money burned. They need written tasks marked by error category and a fortnightly rule. They often resist this, because the sessions are less enjoyable than talking, and the grade movement is nonetheless the fastest of the three profiles.

The second is the diligent Year 7 starter. Accurate written French within a limited range, careful grammar, and a speaking test they are quietly terrified of. This student needs recorded speaking rehearsal on unseen prompts and explicit permission to be imperfect out loud, plus the paraphrase and hesitation devices that let them keep going when a word is missing. The third is the student with a genuine comprehension gap, usually a late starter or someone who missed a year through a school move, and the honest answer there is that the work is vocabulary volume and reading mileage rather than technique. That profile takes longer and costs more, and anyone promising a quick transformation is not being straight with you.
bullets: Heritage speaker: marked written tasks, one rule a fortnight, not conversation
Year 7 starter: recorded speaking rehearsal and recovery strategies
Late starter with a real gap: vocabulary volume and reading mileage, over months

sections.heading: What a 0520 grade is worth in the UAE, and what it is not
paragraphs: For UAE Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects, which is a point that catches many Dubai families out. A modern foreign language such as French is not excluded in the same way, so a 0520 grade can contribute to that count in a way an Arabic grade cannot.

That rule should be read as a planning input rather than as advice, and it should be verified for your own case on moe.gov.ae or with the relevant attestation authority before any decision is made. Equivalency is a Ministry process. IB Gram describes it, points you at the official channel, and does not perform or guarantee any part of it. One competitor page currently ranking in this market states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced figure is five, and it is worth knowing which of those two numbers you are planning around.

Beyond equivalency, a French grade does work that is harder to quantify. It is a prerequisite or a strong preference for several humanities and international-relations routes, it is the entry condition for A Level or IB continuation, and in a city with the professional profile Dubai has it is genuinely used. What it is not is a requirement for tutoring. Nobody needs a tutor to achieve equivalency, nobody needs one to progress at school, and any provider implying that a regulatory process depends on buying lessons is manufacturing urgency about something a ministry administers.

sections.heading: Session count by starting point, and the honest timeline
paragraphs: The most useful number a family can be given is total taught hours, not hourly rate, and almost nobody publishes it. A brief that needs twelve hours at a higher rate costs less than one needing thirty at a lower rate, and finishes sooner. What follows is the range our own 0520 briefs actually run to, by starting profile, and it is a range rather than a promise.

A heritage speaker with a written accuracy problem usually needs eight to fourteen hours across a term, concentrated on marked tasks with a fortnightly rule. A Year 7 starter with a speaking problem needs six to ten hours of recorded rehearsal, which can be delivered in thirty-minute sessions twice a week rather than hour-long ones, and often costs less per week as a result. A student with a genuine comprehension gap needs twenty-five to forty hours over two or three terms, because reading mileage and vocabulary breadth cannot be compressed. A student who is simply unpractised at the exam format, with no underlying weakness, sometimes needs four hours and nothing more, and we will say so.

Timing against the Cambridge calendar matters as much as the count. Cambridge runs IGCSE exams in a June series and a November series, and the entry decisions sit months ahead of the papers. Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries at 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, which illustrates the general pattern: by the time a family starts feeling urgency, the administrative decisions have usually already been made. Working backwards from the entry deadline rather than forwards from today is free and changes the plan.

process.title: Send the mock paper, not just the grade
process.description: A mock grade tells us nothing useful; the paper tells us everything. With the actual script in front of us we can say within minutes whether this is a listening-technique problem, a written-accuracy problem or a genuine comprehension gap, which are three different plans at three different costs.

process.title: Free thirty-minute diagnostic across all four skills
process.description: A short listening set, a timed reading item, one written task and a recorded spoken response. You get a written note naming the weakest component, the specific error categories found, and an estimate of total taught hours. No card details, one trial per family, no obligation to book.

process.title: Pick the component, then the slot
process.description: Sessions are built around one component at a time, because a session that touches all four achieves little in any of them. Speaking rehearsal and written accuracy run best as separate formats, and speaking often works better as two short sessions a week than one long one.

process.title: Lessons online, marked work every fortnight
process.description: One to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a written task set and returned marked on a fortnightly cycle and errors grouped by named category. Every six sessions we send a short written review that can recommend changing focus, changing tutor, or stopping.

whyPoints.title: The diagnosis comes before the hours
whyPoints.description: A 0520 grade is held down by one component far more often than by general weakness, and the four components need opposite interventions. We name the component and the error categories in the first session rather than selling a weekly slot and hoping.

whyPoints.title: Syllabus detail checked, not remembered
whyPoints.description: Component structure, weightings and timings are confirmed against cambridgeinternational.org for your child's exam year, because Cambridge revises these by cohort. We also tell you to ask your exams officer which of the six administrative zones your centre sits in.

whyPoints.title: Speaking rehearsed on record
whyPoints.description: The component least practised in a Dubai classroom and the hardest to improve by advice. Recorded with consent, played back, and measured as time to first response and length of unprompted turn rather than described in adjectives.

whyPoints.title: Marking that names the rule
whyPoints.description: Errors grouped into named categories with a count, one rule targeted per fortnight until the category stops appearing, and the rewritten version always produced by the student. A script covered in undifferentiated red ink teaches nobody anything.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what tutoring cannot do
whyPoints.description: A genuine comprehension gap takes terms rather than weeks, no tutor can promise a grade, and sometimes the right advice is four hours of exam-format practice and nothing more. We also say plainly that nobody needs tutoring to satisfy a Ministry process.

faqs.question: What does Cambridge IGCSE French 0520 actually assess?
faqs.answer: Listening, reading, speaking and writing, as four separately assessed components carrying equal weight on the current syllabus, with every task drawn from five topic areas: everyday activities, personal and social life, the world around us, the world of work, and the international world. Confirm the exact component numbering, timings and mark totals for your child's exam year on cambridgeinternational.org, because Cambridge revises these by cohort. The practical consequence of equal weighting is that fixing the weakest skill moves the grade faster than improving the strongest one.

faqs.question: Which 0520 component do Dubai students lose the most marks on?
faqs.answer: It splits by profile rather than falling on one paper. Students with francophone backgrounds lose most in writing, on silent endings their ear never flags: auxiliary choice, past participle agreement, the partitive after a negative. Students who began French in Year 7 lose most in speaking, through long silences and scripts that collapse under an unexpected follow-up. Across both groups, listening marks go to negation, numbers and the option that is mentioned and then rejected. A session should begin by establishing which of those patterns applies, because the cures share nothing.

faqs.question: My child speaks French at home but keeps getting a 6 in 0520. Why?
faqs.answer: Because written French at IGCSE is marked on accuracy, and spoken French hides exactly the errors the mark scheme catches. Past participle agreement, the choice between etre and avoir in the perfect tense, adjective endings and accents that change meaning are all silent or nearly silent in speech, so a fluent speaker gets no feedback from their own ear. This profile improves faster than any other once the marking is right: short tasks marked by named error category, one rule per fortnight, and the rewrite produced by the student. Conversation practice does nothing here.

faqs.question: How do we prepare for the 0520 speaking test properly?
faqs.answer: By rehearsing the unpredictable part, which is what students skip. Part of the test is a prepared topic and part is unrehearsed conversation across the syllabus areas, and the common failure is a memorised presentation delivered well followed by silence on an unexpected question. Record the rehearsal with consent, ask follow-ups the student has not seen, and play back the moment fluency collapsed. Measure time to first response and length of unprompted turn. Teach French paraphrase and hesitation devices so there is something to say when a word is missing.

faqs.question: Why does my child score badly on 0520 listening despite good French?
faqs.answer: Almost always technique rather than language. Three patterns account for most of it. Negation, where the speaker says they no longer do something and the student answers the first half of the sentence. Numbers, times and prices, which are the easiest marks on the paper and the most commonly lost because French numbers above sixty are constructed rather than named. And the rejected distractor, where an option is mentioned then dismissed and the student picks it. The fix is answering, marking and logging items by cause, not playing French audio in the background.

faqs.question: Is reading practice or vocabulary learning better for the 0520 reading paper?
faqs.answer: Neither, on its own. The reading paper paraphrases systematically, so the habit of scanning for the word that matches the question starts producing confident wrong answers at this level. The exercise that works is covering the text and asking the student to list three ways the idea could be expressed in French before looking, which builds meaning-matching and exposes the recognition vocabulary gaps that actually matter. Add timed sets with questions read first, since students who read every text fully run out of time on the harder final items.

faqs.question: How many hours of 0520 tutoring does a Dubai student usually need?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the profile, and total hours matter more than the hourly rate. A heritage speaker with a written accuracy problem typically needs eight to fourteen hours in a term. A Year 7 starter with a speaking problem needs six to ten hours, often better delivered as two short sessions a week. A student with a genuine comprehension gap needs twenty-five to forty hours over two or three terms, because reading mileage cannot be compressed. A student simply unfamiliar with the exam format sometimes needs four hours, and we will tell you that.

faqs.question: Do you cover both Cambridge 0520 and the Edexcel International GCSE in French?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the distinction matters more than families expect. The two boards differ in component structure, in how speaking is conducted and in series availability, so a tutor working from the wrong board's specification will drill the wrong task formats. Ask your school's exams officer which board and which syllabus code your child is entered for, and bring that detail to the first session. Pearson publishes provisional and final timetables for its International GCSE series on its own site, and those should be read there rather than taken from any tutoring page.

faqs.question: Does a 0520 French grade count towards UAE Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: On the British track the Ministry requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are excluded from that count of five; a modern foreign language is not excluded in the same way, so French can contribute. Verify your own position on moe.gov.ae or with the relevant attestation authority before deciding anything. Equivalency is a Ministry process that no tutoring company performs, and no tutoring is required for it.

faqs.question: Should my child continue to A Level French or IB French B after 0520?
faqs.answer: The deciding evidence is usually the speaking profile rather than the written grade. Cambridge AS and A Level French moves towards texts and extended argued writing, where register is the step up. IB French B assesses intercultural understanding alongside language and leans harder on the individual oral. Students who coped well with the 0520 speaking format tend to find the IB oral manageable; students who scraped through it should think carefully. Confirm current component codes with your exams officer, since Cambridge runs more than one French qualification at this level.

faqs.question: How much does a Cambridge IGCSE French tutor cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published rates across the Dubai market run from roughly AED 45 an hour at the budget online end to AED 650 for a premium named tutor, with qualified subject teachers online generally between AED 150 and 300 and specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. Those are market figures read from provider sites in October 2026, not an IB Gram price list. French usually sits lower in those bands than Arabic, because the teaching pool in this city is considerably deeper. Ask what is inside the hour before comparing any two numbers.

faqs.question: Are 0520 lessons delivered at our home in Dubai or online?
faqs.answer: Online, one to one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not arrange home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring at a UAE address is not a service we sell, and home visiting is offered only in India. For 0520 the format is an advantage rather than a concession: speaking rehearsal can be recorded and replayed, written work lives in a shared document with its version history intact, and the tutor is chosen on marking record rather than on how far they are willing to drive.

faqs.question: Can a tutor correct the French my child hands in to school?
faqs.answer: A tutor can teach, model, question, mark and give feedback. A tutor cannot supply sentences for submission, and cannot improve a piece of assessed work to the point where the French is no longer the student's own. The working rule we apply is that after feedback the student rewrites, and the tutor never types into the submission. If a correction cannot be explained so the student can apply it unaided next time, the correction was pitched at the wrong level and the teaching needs changing, not the script.

faqs.question: When are Cambridge IGCSE French exams held, and when do entries close?
faqs.answer: Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series each year, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Entry deadlines sit months before the papers: Cambridge's published key dates for the March 2027 series put final entries at 27 November 2026 against an exam period of 3 February to 4 March 2027, with results on Direct on 13 May. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting 0520 support in Year 9 rather than Year 11?
faqs.answer: For most students yes, and for a specific reason. Years 7 to 9 are when tense formation either becomes automatic or becomes a permanent weakness, and automaticity is what the productive components reward. Three tenses handled securely at the end of Year 9 is worth more at 0520 than six tenses half-known in Year 11. Early support is also cheaper per outcome because it is short and infrequent: a fortnightly session on verb drilling and reading aloud costs a fraction of a Year 11 block and does more for the eventual grade.

dubai/cambridge-igcse-french-0520-tutor.closingHeading: Bring the mock paper to the first conversation
dubai/cambridge-igcse-french-0520-tutor.closingBody: The fastest way to get value out of a French tutor is to arrive with the script rather than the grade. A mock mark of 62 per cent tells nobody anything; the paper shows within minutes whether the marks went to negation in listening, word-matching in reading, silence in speaking or silent endings in writing, and those are four different plans at four different prices. Thirty free minutes, a short task in each skill, a written note naming the weakest component and the error categories found, and an estimate of total taught hours rather than an hourly rate. No card details, one trial per family. If four hours of exam-format practice is the honest answer, that is the answer you will get.
